stem: Mile stone: A child accompanied by his parents walked into the examination room. He is holding a ball. The doctor asks to let him see the ball; he threw the ball towards the doctor. Then he reaches out to catch it when the doctor threw the ball back to him. He draws a straight line on the paper and then picks up a few blocks from the floor and stacks one on the top of the other. What is the most likely developmental month for this child?
highlight_terms_source: stacks one on the top of the other
why_right: The child throws a ball, reaches out to catch it, draws a line and stacks blocks. Stacking two cubes is a 15 month skill, but catching with extended hands is an 18 month skill, and throwing and line drawing push the child to the upper end; 18 months is the highest option consistent with all of them.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 9 months the child is sitting and pulling to stand with a pincer grasp developing; throwing, catching, drawing and stacking are far beyond this age.
B. At 12 months the child walks with one hand held and has a mature pincer grasp; stacking cubes (15 months) and catching (18 months) are not yet expected.
C. 15 months fits stacking two cubes, but catching with extended hands is an 18 month skill, so 15 underestimates this child.
key_concept:
Milestone questions: the most advanced skill sets the age.
  • 12 months: walks with one hand held, pincer grasp
  • 15 months: stacks 2 cubes, inserts pellet in bottle
  • 18 months: catches with extended hands
  • 2 years: throws overhand, copies lines
exam_pearl: Pick the age of the highest milestone the child shows, not the earliest one.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall: 'Mile stone draw straight line and throw ball'; fuller version from screenshot on next page marked **D. 18.

stem: 65 yo male came complaining with sudden lower fossa pain that is increasing. Labs: Wbc 23, Hb normal. CT shows diverticulitis + collection. What is the initial and most appropriate?
why_right: CT shows diverticulitis with a collection (a diverticular abscess, Hinchey I or II) and the stem does not describe generalized peritonitis or instability. A drainable abscess (about 4 cm or more) is treated with IV antibiotics plus image guided percutaneous drainage, which is both the initial and the most appropriate step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Laparoscopy: reserved for failed percutaneous drainage, an undrainable abscess, or purulent peritonitis (Hinchey III) where laparoscopic lavage or resection is considered.
B. Open laparotomy: for perforated diverticulitis with generalized (purulent or feculent) peritonitis, Hinchey III or IV, or an unstable patient; not for a contained, drainable collection.
key_concept:
Diverticulitis management by Hinchey stage.
  • Uncomplicated: antibiotics (or observation if mild and immunocompetent)
  • Small abscess (about 3 cm or less): IV antibiotics alone
  • Larger abscess (about 4 cm or more): percutaneous drainage + antibiotics
  • Purulent or feculent peritonitis: surgery (laparotomy, Hartmann)
  • After recovery: colonoscopy at 6 to 8 weeks to exclude cancer
exam_pearl: A contained collection is drained through the skin; free perforation with peritonitis goes to theatre.
compiler_note:
Terse recall of the same question: Diverticulitis with fluid collection about 20/13 cm what to do next??
Compiler note: Compiler typed 'A. Percutaneous drain.' under the recall. Rule: 4 cm -> drain; 3 cm -> conservative (if there is fever or SIRS, choose IV Abx over conservative). Options taken from the 'Diverticulosis with collection management' restatement.

stem: Q: Patient with acute diverticulitis fluid collection What is your next step
key_concept:
Diverticular collection: size and sepsis decide.
  • Small collection: IV antibiotics (conservative)
  • Larger collection (about 4 cm or more): percutaneous drainage + antibiotics
  • Generalized peritonitis: laparotomy
  • Colonoscopy: 6 to 8 weeks later, never in the acute phase
exam_pearl: Colonoscopy is the right answer only when the stem says the attack has resolved.

stem: baby with recurrent migraine for 2 weeks daily what to give given initial treatment with no effect what next?
key_concept:
Migraine: treat the attack, then prevent if attacks are frequent.
  • Acute, mild to moderate: NSAID (ibuprofen) or paracetamol
  • Acute, moderate to severe: triptan
  • Frequent or daily attacks, or acute therapy failing: start prophylaxis
  • Prophylaxis options: beta blocker, amitriptyline (TCA), others
  • Daily analgesic use risks medication overuse headache
exam_pearl: Decide by pattern: single attack = acute analgesic; frequent or daily attacks failing acute therapy = prophylaxis; heartburn or epigastric pain = PPI.

stem: A 19-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of frequent attacks of per-rectal fresh bleeding. Physical examination confirmed clotted blood in the rectum. Nasogastric tube was draining greenish coloured fluids. Hb 85. Colonoscopy: no colorectal pathology. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic tool to localize source of bleeding?
why_right: A 19-year-old with painless recurrent fresh rectal bleeding, a nasogastric tube draining bile (greenish fluid) that argues against an upper GI source, and a normal colonoscopy points to a small bowel source, most likely a Meckel diverticulum. A technetium 99m pertechnetate (Meckel) scan localizes it by detecting ectopic gastric mucosa.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diagnostic laparoscopy: may be used to confirm and resect a Meckel diverticulum once suspected, but it is invasive and not the first test to localize bleeding.
B. Gastrografin follow through: a contrast study for obstruction or fistula; it does not show the bleeding point or the ectopic gastric mucosa.
C. Upper GI endoscopy: first line when an upper source is suspected (melena, blood in the NG aspirate); here bilious NG drainage makes an upper source unlikely.
key_concept:
Bleeding with negative colonoscopy: think small bowel.
  • Young, painless bright red bleeding: Meckel scan (Tc 99m pertechnetate)
  • Bilious NG aspirate without blood: upper source unlikely
  • Older, stable, negative EGD and colonoscopy: capsule endoscopy
  • Active brisk bleeding: CT angiography or tagged RBC scan
exam_pearl: Meckel rule of 2: about 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, presents before age 2, may contain gastric or pancreatic tissue.

stem: 16 years old female presented to the ER after sustaining a trauma due to fall from 10 metres height; she identifies site of pain by moaning; what is the best way to secure Airway?
highlight_terms_source: identifies site of pain by moaning
why_right: A fall from 10 metres with a patient who only moans and merely localises pain has a depressed conscious level and cannot protect her airway, which is an indication for a definitive airway. In trauma the definitive airway is a cuffed tube in the trachea, i.e. endotracheal intubation (done orally with manual in-line cervical spine stabilisation). This recall's key is the general term "endotracheal" as the definitive, aspiration-protecting airway.
why_wrong_block:
B. Nasotracheal: a blind technique that is unsafe after major head and facial trauma (possible base of skull fracture, bleeding) and needs a breathing patient; it is not the trauma airway of choice.
C. Orotracheal: this is in fact the usual route of endotracheal intubation in trauma; the recall keys the broader term "endotracheal", so learn the key as the definitive cuffed tube in the trachea.
key_concept:
Trauma airway: who needs a definitive airway and which one.
  • Indications: GCS 8 or less / unconscious, SpO2 <88%, risk of aspiration (oral bleeding, secretions)
  • Default: endotracheal (oral) intubation with in-line C-spine stabilisation
  • Intubation needed + severe facial injury (e.g. mandibular fracture) = cricothyroidotomy
  • Avoid nasotracheal route with suspected base of skull or midface fracture
exam_pearl: Add severe facial or mandibular injury to the stem and the answer flips from endotracheal intubation to cricothyroidotomy.

stem: child was hit by a car how to assess consciousness:
OptC: he can mention what was happen exactly
key_concept:
Level of consciousness after head or multiple trauma = GCS (pediatric GCS in young children).
  • Eye 4, Verbal 5, Motor 6; total 3 to 15
  • Verbal 5 = oriented to time, place, person
  • GCS below 15 or altered mental status: head CT (PECARN)
  • AVPU is a quick bedside alternative in primary survey
exam_pearl: Orientation is only one piece (the verbal score) of the full consciousness assessment.

stem: Pt with massive hematemesis all are normal except WBC and Blood urea nitrogen is high diagnosis ?
why_right: Peptic ulcer disease is the most common cause of hematemesis, and a massive bleed fits an ulcer eroding into a vessel (e.g. a posterior duodenal ulcer and the gastroduodenal artery). The raised BUN with otherwise normal labs reflects digested blood protein absorbed from the gut, a marker of upper GI bleeding, not liver or kidney disease. With no alcohol, liver or vomiting clue, PUD is the default answer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Erosive gastritis: usually causes low-volume oozing; it is the classic answer in an alcoholic or NSAID/stress setting, which the stem does not give.
C. Mallory-Weiss syndrome: needs a history of forceful or repeated vomiting before the hematemesis; that trigger is absent here.
D. Esophageal varices: right when there are signs of chronic liver disease or portal hypertension (alcohol, abnormal LFTs, ascites, splenomegaly); here everything except WBC and BUN is normal.
key_concept:
Upper GI bleed: pick the cause from the history clue.
  • No clue / default = peptic ulcer disease (most common)
  • Vomiting first, then blood = Mallory-Weiss tear
  • Liver disease, portal hypertension = varices
  • Alcohol binge, NSAIDs, ICU stress = erosive gastritis
  • High BUN with normal creatinine = blood digested in the upper GI tract
exam_pearl: An isolated high BUN in a bleeding patient points to an upper GI source, not renal failure.

stem: baby 2 y with diarrhea. Mother concerned about her brother 1y/o How to prevent?
why_right: Infectious diarrhea in children spreads mainly by the fecal-oral route and close household contact, so the way to protect the "1y/o" brother is to interrupt transmission. Hand washing with soap (after diaper changes and toilet use, before preparing food and feeding) is the simplest and most effective preventive measure.
why_wrong_block: B. Prophylactic probiotics are not recommended to prevent transmission to contacts; probiotics are at most considered as an adjunct to shorten diarrhea in the affected child, not as household prevention.
key_concept:
Preventing spread of childhood diarrhea: break fecal-oral transmission.
  • Hand washing with soap: single best measure
  • Safe water and food hygiene
  • Proper diaper disposal, clean surfaces
  • Rotavirus vaccine for primary prevention in infants
  • Affected child: ORS and continue feeding
exam_pearl: "How to prevent" in a contact = hygiene, not a drug.

stem: Patient with 3 day hx of colectomy present with fever and tenderness mainly LLQ and have abdominal distension + absent bowel sound Asking about most initial study
why_right: On day 3 after colectomy the patient has distension and absent bowel sounds with fever and LLQ tenderness: the first question is ileus or obstruction versus a complication such as an anastomotic leak. The lead-in asks for the most initial study, and a plain abdominal X-ray is the quick bedside first image to show dilated loops, air-fluid levels or gross free air. This recall's key is the plain film as the first imaging step, with CT as the follow-on test.
why_wrong_block:
B. CBC + lactate: useful bloods for sepsis and ischemia and usually drawn alongside, but the recall treats the question as asking for the first imaging study.
C. Re-exploration: reserved for a clear surgical emergency (generalised peritonitis, hemodynamic instability, a confirmed large leak); no instability is described here, so you investigate first.
key_concept:
Post-operative distension with absent bowel sounds: is it ileus, obstruction or a leak?
  • Ileus: check and correct electrolytes (especially potassium), bowel rest, NG tube
  • Plain abdominal X-ray: first quick image for distension
  • Suspected anastomotic leak (fever, focal peritonism after day 3 to 5): CT with contrast
  • Unstable or generalised peritonitis: return to theatre
exam_pearl: Free air on X-ray is expected for some days after open abdominal surgery, so it does not by itself prove a leak.

stem: A 5-week-old infant is brought by the mother after having sudden jerky movements involving upper and lower limbs. The infant was managed acutely with IV calcium. He is now stable and doing well. What is the most appropriate advice?
why_right: A "5-week-old" with jerky movements that needed "IV calcium" had a hypocalcemic seizure; in early infancy this is commonly due to vitamin D deficiency (often from a vitamin D deficient mother and exclusive breastfeeding). After acute correction, the underlying cause must be treated, so the advice is vitamin D supplementation (with calcium as needed) to prevent recurrence.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance alone ignores the cause; without vitamin D the hypocalcemia and seizures can recur. Reassurance fits benign events (e.g. normal newborn stool patterns), not a treated hypocalcemic seizure.
C. Avoiding sun is the opposite of what is needed: sunlight makes vitamin D in the skin. Sun avoidance is advised for photosensitive conditions, not for vitamin D deficiency.
key_concept:
Infant hypocalcemic seizure: correct calcium acutely, then treat the cause.
  • Common cause in early infancy: vitamin D deficiency (maternal deficiency, exclusive breastfeeding)
  • Nutritional vitamin D deficiency: low or normal Ca, low phosphate, high ALP, high PTH, low 25-OH vitamin D
  • Prevention: routine vitamin D for breastfed infants (400 IU/day)
  • Also check and treat the mother
exam_pearl: Once the seizure is controlled, "most appropriate advice" targets the cause: vitamin D, not reassurance.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presented to the ED with 18-hour history of severe epigastric pain associated with vomiting. She is known to have multiple small gallstones. Upper abdominal tenderness. Labs: WBC 13.4; ALP 289; Amylase 488; Direct bilirubin 19; Total bilirubin 34. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: Severe epigastric pain with vomiting and amylase 488 (more than 3 times normal) in a woman with multiple small gallstones is acute gallstone pancreatitis. The lead-in asks for the most appropriate initial management, and the first priority is early IV crystalloid resuscitation (Ringer lactate preferred), together with analgesia. Everything else follows once fluids are running.
why_wrong_block:
A. Abdominal ultrasound: done to confirm the gallstone cause and assess the CBD, but it is an investigation, not the initial management; the diagnosis is already made on pain plus enzymes.
C. Broad-spectrum antibiotics: not given routinely in acute pancreatitis; right when there is cholangitis or infected necrosis.
D. ERCP: right for gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction (e.g. dilated CBD, rising jaundice); the mildly raised bilirubin here does not demand it as the first step.
key_concept:
Acute pancreatitis = 2 of 3: typical pain, amylase/lipase ≥3x normal, imaging findings.
  • Initial: IV crystalloid (Ringer lactate), analgesia
  • Ultrasound: look for gallstones / CBD dilation
  • Urgent ERCP: only with cholangitis or persistent CBD obstruction
  • Antibiotics: only for infection (cholangitis, infected necrosis)
  • Mild biliary pancreatitis: cholecystectomy in the same admission
exam_pearl: Add fever plus jaundice (cholangitis) and the answer moves to antibiotics and ERCP.

stem: Child has severe pain in lower abdomen with guarding and the pain is in the groin area, what is the next appropriate step ?
highlight_terms_source: pain is in the groin area
why_right: In a child (implied boy) with severe lower abdominal pain radiating to the groin, testicular torsion must be excluded first, because it often presents as abdominal or groin pain and boys may not report scrotal pain. A genital (scrotal) examination is fast, bedside and can reveal a high-riding, tender testis with absent cremasteric reflex, or an incarcerated inguinal hernia. The time-critical lesion is found by examination, not by imaging.
why_wrong_block: B. CT: radiation in a child and a delay that can cost the testis; right only after examination for intra-abdominal causes when the diagnosis is still unclear. Doppler ultrasound, not CT, is the imaging for the scrotum.
key_concept:
Boy with lower abdominal or groin pain: examine the genitalia and groin every time.
  • Torsion: sudden severe pain, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex: urgent surgical exploration
  • Incarcerated inguinal hernia: tender irreducible groin lump
  • Equivocal torsion: Doppler ultrasound, without delaying surgery
  • Other alternatives a student may consider: abdominal exam for appendicitis, urinalysis
exam_pearl: Torsion in children often presents as abdominal pain; skipping the scrotal exam is the classic missed diagnosis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Similar screenshot (male child with sudden lower abdominal and groin pain, which is most important to be examined: A-Abdominal exam, B-Groin exam, C-General exam) shows Answer: B. Alhomrani: if option C was 'GENITAL' then go for it (genital, not general).

stem: Newborn in 3rd percentile, family poor was diluting formula milk, what is next most appropriate?
OptC: Advice family how to make formula
why_right: This recall's key is hospitalization: a newborn already at the "3rd percentile" with weight faltering from diluted formula has little reserve, and over-dilution also risks dilutional hyponatremia and seizures. With a "poor family" who may not be able to afford proper feeds, advice alone may fail, so admission allows supervised feeding, documentation of intake and weight gain, labs, and social work involvement.
why_wrong_block:
B. High-calorie formula treats inadequate calorie intake when the family feeds correctly, or when increased needs exist (e.g. cardiac disease); it does not fix the cause here (wrong preparation, poverty), and concentrated feeds in a newborn need supervision.
C. Teaching correct formula preparation is right when a stable infant with mild weight faltering has a simple preparation error and a family able to follow advice with close outpatient follow-up; the key here treats this newborn as needing admission first.
key_concept:
Failure to thrive from inadequate intake: decide outpatient vs inpatient.
  • Outpatient: mild, stable, reliable family, simple fixable cause (education, follow-up)
  • Admit: severe malnutrition, dehydration or electrolyte disturbance (diluted formula: hyponatremia), very young infant, failed outpatient care, neglect or safety concern
  • Always involve dietitian and social work when poverty drives the problem
exam_pearl: Diluted formula in a newborn can cause hyponatremic seizures, not just poor growth.

stem: Newborn with meconium aspiration syndrome has hypoxia and severe respiratory distress. What is the most appropriate management?
OptB: Intubation and mechanical ventilation if needed
why_right: Meconium aspiration syndrome with "hypoxia and severe respiratory distress" means respiratory failure. The newborn needs a secured airway with intubation and mechanical ventilation (plus surfactant and, if hypoxemia persists, inhaled nitric oxide or ECMO for pulmonary hypertension).
why_wrong_block: A. Supplemental oxygen with noninvasive positive pressure suits mild to moderate distress with adequate oxygenation; in severe MAS it is insufficient, and positive pressure without control can worsen air trapping and air leak (pneumothorax).
key_concept:
MAS management follows severity.
  • Mild: oxygen to target saturations, supportive care
  • Moderate: CPAP/noninvasive support with caution (air leak risk)
  • Severe or respiratory failure: intubation and mechanical ventilation
  • Adjuncts: surfactant, iNO for PPHN, HFOV, ECMO if refractory
  • Routine tracheal suctioning of non-vigorous infants is no longer recommended
exam_pearl: In a newborn with MAS, "severe" distress plus hypoxia = respiratory failure = intubate and ventilate; oxygen or CPAP is for milder cases.

stem: Boot heart shape in xray, Most appropriate next investigation
key_concept:
Tetralogy of Fallot work-up.
  • CXR: boot-shaped heart, decreased pulmonary markings
  • ECG: right axis deviation, RVH
  • Confirmatory: transthoracic echocardiography
  • Further anatomy if needed: CT/MR angiography or catheterization
  • Definitive: surgical repair at 3 to 6 months
  • Tet spell: knee to chest, oxygen, morphine, fluids, beta blocker
exam_pearl: If echo is offered, it beats every other option as the next investigation for a boot-shaped heart.

stem: 14-year-old male, diarrhea for 3 months, associated with abdominal bloating and loss of subcutaneous fat. What is the best treatment?
why_right: Chronic diarrhea ("3 months") with bloating and loss of subcutaneous fat (with a faltering growth chart) points to malabsorption, and in this setting celiac disease is the classic cause. Its treatment is a lifelong gluten free diet.
why_wrong_block:
A. A hydrolyzed (extensively hydrolyzed protein) diet is for cow's milk protein allergy, mainly in infants; not a 14-year-old with chronic malabsorption.
C. A high-calorie diet suits undernutrition from inadequate intake (e.g. marasmus); here the problem is malabsorption, so extra calories are lost unless gluten is removed.
D. A fat free diet does not treat celiac disease; fat restriction (with MCT) is used for conditions such as intestinal lymphangiectasia or chylous leaks, not gluten enteropathy.
key_concept:
Celiac disease: chronic diarrhea + bloating + poor growth/weight loss.
  • Initial test: IgA anti-tTG (with total IgA), anti-endomysial antibody
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy)
  • Keep gluten in the diet until testing is done
  • Associations: dermatitis herpetiformis, iron deficiency, type 1 diabetes
  • Treatment: lifelong gluten free diet
exam_pearl: Do not start the gluten free diet before serology and biopsy: it causes false negative results.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A growth chart image was shown with it (per recaller).

stem: Girl with webbed neck, short stature, broad chest and widely spaced nipples. What to do next?
key_concept:
Turner syndrome: diagnose by karyotype, then screen and treat.
  • Clues: short stature, webbed neck, low hairline, shield chest, widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, primary amenorrhea
  • Diagnosis: karyotype 45,X (or mosaic)
  • Screen: echo (coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve), renal US (horseshoe kidney), thyroid
  • Treatment: growth hormone, estrogen replacement
  • A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to chromosomal analysis.
exam_pearl: Confirm before you treat: karyotype comes before growth hormone.

stem: Pediatric 13 years of age, chest pain and other cardiac symptoms (dyspnea on exertion), and ASO = 800. How long will he use penicillin?
why_right: A "13 years" old with cardiac symptoms (chest pain, dyspnea on exertion) and a high ASO (800) has rheumatic fever with carditis. Secondary prophylaxis for carditis without residual heart disease is 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer: 13 + 10 = 23 years, which is longer than 21.
why_wrong_block:
B. Age 21 would be the stopping point only if "until 21" were longer than 10 years, i.e. in younger children with carditis (or for rheumatic fever without carditis); here 10 years carries him to 23.
C. Age 15 gives only 2 years of prophylaxis, below even the minimum for rheumatic fever without carditis (5 years or until 21).
key_concept:
Secondary prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin, after the last attack): take whichever is LONGER.
  • No carditis: 5 years or until age 21
  • Carditis, no residual heart disease: 10 years or until age 21
  • Carditis with residual valvular disease: 10 years or until age 40, lifetime may be needed
exam_pearl: Always compute both (age + years vs the age cutoff) and pick the later one; residual valve disease pushes the cutoff to 40.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recaller forgot the last option. Answer bar: 23 years old.

stem: Baby (2 months old) was diagnosed with congenital heart disease came to the ER with bluish discoloration, the mother said he was crying. What will you do?
key_concept:
Cyanosis with crying in a CHD infant: calm and reassess first, escalate only if it persists.
  • Cyanosis worse with crying or feeding = classic tetralogy of Fallot picture
  • Tet spell first aid: calm baby, knee-chest position, oxygen
  • Persistent spell: sedation and further medical treatment, then urgent cardiology
  • Back to baseline after calming: home with cardiology follow-up
  • Cyanotic CHD: TOF, TGA, tricuspid atresia, truncus arteriosus
exam_pearl: Cyanosis that appears only with crying settles when the baby is calmed; cyanosis that persists after calming, oxygen and knee-chest position is a true spell that needs escalation.

stem: 7 year old child fully vaccinated fall in the park presented with clean and small wound. What to do?
why_right: A fully vaccinated 7-year-old with a clean, small wound needs no tetanus prophylaxis: his last tetanus-containing dose (DTaP at school entry in the national schedule) is well within the 10-year window that applies to clean minor wounds. So after simple wound cleaning, reassurance is all that is needed.
why_wrong_block:
B. A tetanus booster for a clean minor wound is given only if vaccination is incomplete/unknown or the last dose was over 10 years ago (over 5 years for a dirty or tetanus-prone wound); neither applies to this child.
C. Tetanus immunoglobulin is for tetanus-prone (dirty, deep, devitalised) wounds in a person with fewer than 3 doses or unknown vaccine history; a fully vaccinated child with a clean wound does not need it.
D. Vaccine plus immunoglobulin together is for a dirty or tetanus-prone wound in an incompletely or unknown immunised patient; it is excessive here.
key_concept:
Tetanus prophylaxis depends on wound type and vaccine history.
  • Clean minor wound, 3 or more doses: booster only if last dose over 10 years ago
  • Dirty/tetanus-prone wound, 3 or more doses: booster if last dose over 5 years ago
  • Fewer than 3 doses or unknown: give vaccine; add TIG only if wound is dirty/tetanus-prone
  • TIG is for exposure, never routine prevention
exam_pearl: Change the wound to dirty or the history to unknown/incomplete and the answer moves to vaccine, or vaccine plus TIG.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option D was recalled in Arabic as 'I think it was both the vaccine and the immunoglobulin'.

stem: 4-month child: delayed motor, hypotonia + reduced reflexes + antigravity muscles weak, CK normal, myopathic pattern on (EMG?).
key_concept:
Floppy infant: localise with reflexes, CK and EMG.
  • SMA: areflexia, tongue fasciculations, CK normal, EMG neurogenic, SMN1 gene test
  • Congenital myopathy: reflexes reduced, CK normal or mildly raised, EMG myopathic, diagnosis by biopsy
  • Congenital muscular dystrophy: CK markedly raised, EMG myopathic, contractures common
  • Central (brain) hypotonia: reflexes normal or brisk, weakness less marked
exam_pearl: Normal CK plus myopathic EMG points to congenital myopathy; normal CK plus neurogenic EMG and fasciculations points to SMA.

stem: 6-year-old boy with day and night enuresis, his mother mentioned chronic constipation; exam is normal apart from sacral dimples. What should you do?
why_right: This is not simple bedwetting: the child has day and night enuresis plus chronic constipation and a sacral dimple, which together suggest a neurogenic bladder and bowel from occult spinal dysraphism (e.g. tethered cord). The enuresis work-up says daytime symptoms with constipation and a lumbosacral spine abnormality need MRI of the lumbosacral spine to detect a congenital spinal defect.
why_wrong_block:
B. Reassurance fits primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis: night wetting only, no daytime symptoms, normal urinalysis and normal exam. Daytime wetting, constipation and a sacral marker rule that out here.
C. Urinalysis is done in every child with enuresis and is the key test when no red flag is present (it screens for UTI, diabetes and diabetes insipidus), but it cannot find the suspected spinal lesion; the sacral dimple with bladder and bowel dysfunction is the decisive finding.
key_concept:
Enuresis + constipation + spine marker = image the spine.
  • Every child: urinalysis
  • Night only, normal UA and exam: primary monosymptomatic enuresis, reassure
  • Daytime symptoms with constipation/encopresis: look for hypothyroidism, recurrent UTI, spine deformity
  • Recurrent UTI: renal ultrasound and VCUG
  • Lumbosacral deformity or abnormal neuro exam: MRI spine
exam_pearl: Remove the sacral dimple and the daytime symptoms, and the answer becomes urinalysis or reassurance.

stem: A 6 month infant with vertical transmission of HIV, started on antiretroviral therapy and developmentally doing good. Which of the following vaccines needs to be considered?
key_concept:
HIV child: inactivated vaccines always; live vaccines only if not severely immunosuppressed.
  • Viral vaccines are live except hepatitis B, hepatitis A, IPV, HPV and inactivated influenza
  • Inactivated influenza: from 6 months, yearly, recommended in HIV
  • MMR and varicella: live, from 12 months, only with adequate CD4
  • BCG: avoided in HIV-infected infants
  • Hep B, DTaP, PCV, Hib: safe, give per schedule
exam_pearl: In an HIV-infected child, inactivated vaccines are always safe; the live ones (MMR, varicella, BCG) are the ones whose timing depends on age and CD4.

stem: 4 months old came with mild flu symptoms, T 37.1; mother asking about vaccinations?
key_concept:
Mild illness is not a contraindication; vaccinate on schedule.
  • Postpone only for moderate or severe acute illness
  • 2 and 4 months: IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV13, rotavirus
  • 6 months: OPV first appears, plus IPV, DTaP, Hep B, Hib, PCV13
  • 9 months: measles + MCV4
  • 18 months: OPV, DTaP, Hib, MMR, varicella, Hep A
exam_pearl: Runny nose with normal temperature = vaccinate today; only a moderately to severely ill child has vaccines deferred.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 62-year-old man, DM and HTN, presents with 4-hour history of sudden left leg pain, history of claudication at 200 m, smoker for 40 years. Left: femoral present, absent popliteal and distal; right: intact femoral and popliteal but diminished distal pulses. ECG normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
highlight_terms_source: 4-hour history of sudden left leg pain
why_right: Sudden leg pain for 4 hours with absent popliteal and distal pulses on a background of claudication is acute (on chronic) limb ischemia. No sensory or motor loss is described, so the limb is not immediately threatened and there is time to image. The lead-in asks for the most appropriate investigation, i.e. the definitive anatomical test, which is CT angiography.
why_wrong_block:
B. Vascular ultrasound: a reasonable initial bedside screen, but it is not the definitive test that maps the occlusion and run-off for planning.
C. Conventional angiogram: invasive; now used mainly when an endovascular intervention is planned in the same sitting, not as the first diagnostic test.
D. MR angiogram: slower and less available in an acute setting; an alternative when CT contrast is contraindicated.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia ladder: heparin, then image (US first, CT angiography definitive), unless the limb is threatened.
  • 6Ps: pain, pallor, paresthesia, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis
  • Sensory/motor deficit: skip imaging, go to revascularisation
  • AF / cardiac source: embolectomy
  • Atherosclerotic in situ thrombosis: catheter-directed thrombolysis
  • Irreversible ischemia: amputation
exam_pearl: "Initial" step = heparin; "most appropriate investigation" = CT angiography; altered motor exam = no imaging at all.

stem: A 40-year-old healthy woman with 4-hour history of sudden onset right lower limb pain. Intact femoral pulse but absent distal pulses, diminished sensory with altered motor exam. ECG: atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Sudden limb pain with absent distal pulses in a healthy 40-year-old with atrial fibrillation is acute embolic limb ischemia, and the intact femoral pulse places the embolus at or just below the femoral bifurcation. Diminished sensation and altered motor exam mean a threatened limb that needs immediate revascularisation. Embolectomy is the treatment for an embolic occlusion.
why_wrong_block:
B. Above knee amputation: only for irreversible ischemia (fixed mottling, rigid paralysis) or a non-salvageable limb; at 4 hours this limb is still salvageable.
C. Catheter-directed thrombolysis: right for in situ thrombosis on atherosclerotic disease (acute on chronic ischemia) in a limb not yet severely threatened; it acts too slowly when motor function is already altered.
D. Heparinization and observation: heparin is the first step in all acute limb ischemia, but alone it does not restore flow to a threatened limb.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia treatment: decide embolus vs thrombosis.
  • Embolus (AF, healthy vessels, sudden onset): embolectomy
  • Thrombosis (claudication history, diabetes, smoker): catheter-directed thrombolysis
  • Motor or sensory deficit: no imaging, straight to revascularisation
  • Irreversible ischemia: amputation
  • Heparin first in every case
exam_pearl: AF plus a previously healthy patient = embolus = embolectomy; claudication history plus normal ECG = thrombosis = thrombolysis.

stem: A 40-year-old healthy woman with 4-hour history of sudden onset right lower limb pain. Intact femoral pulse but absent distal pulses, diminished sensory with altered motor exam. ECG: atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
why_right: This is acute embolic limb ischemia (AF, sudden onset, absent distal pulses) with diminished sensation and altered motor exam, i.e. a threatened limb. When motor function is affected, imaging is skipped because any delay risks limb loss; the source is clearly embolic, so the patient goes straight to embolectomy. That is why the best "investigation" answer here is no investigation.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT angiogram: the most appropriate investigation for acute limb ischemia when the limb is not threatened (no motor or sensory loss); here it would only delay revascularisation.
B. Vascular ultrasound: the initial imaging in a stable, viable limb; not when motor function is already altered.
C. Conventional angiogram: invasive and time-consuming; it may be done on the table during the procedure but must not delay surgery.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia: the motor exam decides whether to image.
  • Viable limb (no deficit): heparin, ultrasound, then CT angiography
  • Threatened limb (sensory or motor loss): no imaging, immediate revascularisation
  • Embolic (AF): embolectomy
  • Thrombotic (atherosclerosis): catheter-directed thrombolysis
exam_pearl: Same AF scenario without motor or sensory loss and the answer flips back to CT angiogram.

stem: A 62-year-old man, DM HTN, presents with 4-hour history of sudden left leg pain, history of claudication at 200 m, non-compliant, smoker 40 years. Left: femoral present, absent popliteal and distal; right: diminished distal pulses. Elevated BSL. ECG: Normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: A diabetic, hypertensive 40-year smoker with claudication at 200 m and bilateral pulse deficits now has sudden pain for 4 hours with absent popliteal and distal pulses: acute on chronic ischemia from in situ thrombosis on atherosclerotic disease. The normal ECG argues against a cardiac embolus. Thrombosis on diseased vessels is treated with catheter-directed thrombolysis, which also unmasks the underlying lesion for later angioplasty or bypass.
why_wrong_block:
B. Femoral thrombectomy: the operation for a cardiac embolus (e.g. AF) lodged in a healthy artery; with no embolic source and diffusely diseased vessels it is not first choice.
C. Above knee amputation: only for irreversible ischemia or a non-salvageable limb; nothing here suggests that.
D. Heparinization and observation: heparin is the first step but on its own does not reopen an acutely occluded artery.
key_concept:
Embolus vs thrombosis in acute limb ischemia.
  • Thrombosis: claudication history, risk factors, bilateral disease, normal ECG: catheter-directed thrombolysis
  • Embolus: AF or recent MI, sudden, healthy other limb: embolectomy
  • Heparin first in both
  • Irreversible ischemia: amputation
exam_pearl: Change the ECG to atrial fibrillation and the answer becomes embolectomy.

stem: Gravida 41 weeks, child delivered via NVD and had respiratory distress but not saturated. What next?
why_right: A 41-week (late-term) newborn with respiratory distress who is not saturating is hypoxaemic, and the immediate step is supplemental oxygen titrated to target saturation while the cause (meconium aspiration is a concern at this gestation, or TTN) is worked out. Treat the hypoxia first, then investigate and escalate support if oxygen alone fails.
why_wrong_block:
B. Keeping the baby NPO is a reasonable supportive measure in a tachypnoeic neonate to reduce aspiration risk, but it does nothing for the low saturation and is not the next step.
C. Surfactant is for surfactant-deficient RDS in a preterm infant (and sometimes for severe meconium aspiration after intubation); it is not first-line for a term or post-term baby who has only just been started on support.
D. Magnesium sulfate is a maternal drug for preeclampsia/eclampsia and fetal neuroprotection; it has no role as the next step in a hypoxic newborn.
key_concept:
Neonatal respiratory distress with low saturation: oxygen first, then find the cause.
  • Preterm: RDS (surfactant deficiency), may need CPAP and surfactant
  • Term CS: TTN, self-resolving, supportive oxygen
  • Post-term, meconium-stained liquor: meconium aspiration syndrome
  • Escalate oxygen to CPAP/ventilation if saturation does not improve
exam_pearl: Surfactant is the trap: it belongs to the preterm RDS story, not to a 41-week baby whose first need is oxygen.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0237).

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Ultrasound shows a diffusely calcified gallbladder without stones. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: 2-month history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain
why_right: A diffusely calcified gallbladder on ultrasound is a porcelain gallbladder, which is associated with gallbladder carcinoma. This patient is also symptomatic (2 months of RUQ pain), so removal is indicated on both counts. The answer is cholecystectomy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Percutaneous biopsy: not used to work up a suspected gallbladder malignancy because it risks seeding the tract and a negative result does not exclude cancer; resection is diagnostic and therapeutic.
C. Cholecystostomy tube: a temporary drain for acute (often acalculous) cholecystitis in a patient too sick for surgery; it does not treat the cancer risk.
D. Observation: may be discussed only for an asymptomatic patient unfit for surgery; this patient has symptoms.
key_concept:
Gallbladder findings that call for cholecystectomy.
  • Porcelain (calcified) gallbladder: cholecystectomy
  • Symptomatic gallstones / biliary colic: elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
  • Polyp 10 mm or more: cholecystectomy
  • Acalculous cholecystitis in the critically ill: cholecystostomy tube
exam_pearl: Calcified gallbladder wall = cancer risk = remove it; do not biopsy it.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's typed recall: 'Pts complaining of RUQ pain for 2 month, US showing diffuse calcified gall bladder without stones, next?' with A. cholecystectomy highlighted (options: cholecystectomy, percutaneous biopsy, cholecystectomy tube, observation). The 'Q:' restatement lists A-C only; Answer: A- Cholecystectomy.

stem: A 2-month-old baby presented with fever, vomiting, lethargy, and poor oral intake for 2 days. Urine dipstick shows nitrites, leukocytes. What is the most appropriate management?
OptB: Send to hospital and start IV antibiotics
highlight_terms_source: fever, vomiting, lethargy, and poor oral intake
why_right: A 2-month-old with fever, vomiting, lethargy and poor intake plus nitrites and leukocytes has a febrile UTI (likely pyelonephritis, possibly urosepsis). Age under 3 months, a toxic or lethargic appearance and inability to keep oral intake down are each indications for admission and IV antibiotics.
why_wrong_block: A. Oral antibiotics at home suit an older, well-looking child who tolerates oral intake; this young, lethargic, vomiting infant may not absorb oral drugs and is at risk of sepsis, so outpatient oral treatment is unsafe.
key_concept:
Paediatric UTI: admit for IV antibiotics when the child is young or unwell.
  • Age under 3 months
  • Toxic, lethargic or septic appearance
  • Vomiting or unable to tolerate oral intake
  • Otherwise well older child: oral antibiotics as outpatient
  • Send urine culture before starting antibiotics
exam_pearl: Any febrile UTI under 3 months is managed in hospital with IV antibiotics, however well the dipstick story looks.

stem: Female in her 30s underwent carpal tunnel syndrome surgery, when the surgeon applied lidocaine with adrenaline she started to have more pain and numbness, what is the most appropriate initial step? (I'm sure the stem like this)
OptC: Check signs of ischemia in her hand
why_right: Adrenaline in the local anaesthetic is a vasoconstrictor, so new or worsening pain after injection into the hand raises the fear of vasospasm and compromised perfusion. The lead-in is "most appropriate initial step": before any test, you examine the hand at the bedside (colour, temperature, capillary refill, radial/ulnar pulses, digit turgor). The clinical findings then decide whether anything further (reversal with an alpha blocker, imaging) is needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. BP and HR would matter if you suspected systemic adrenaline or anaesthetic toxicity (palpitations, tachycardia, agitation, perioral tingling); the complaint here is local pain and numbness in the operated hand.
B. Doppler US is a second step once examination shows signs of ischemia or is equivocal; imaging never comes before a bedside vascular exam.
key_concept:
Suspected limb or digit ischemia: clinical examination first, imaging second.
  • Check colour, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, pain on passive stretch
  • Local findings (pallor, cold, delayed refill) point to vasospasm or vascular compromise
  • Systemic symptoms (tachycardia, palpitations, CNS signs) point to systemic absorption: then check vitals
  • Examination findings guide whether Doppler or reversal is needed
exam_pearl: "Initial step" in a limb perfusion question = examine the limb, not order the Doppler.

stem: 48 years old male patient known with hyperlipidemia with recurrent history of acute pancreatitis for the last 10 years, presented with vomiting blood 1 day ago, all labs are normal, and on examination, the patient had splenomegaly; on radiological examination, esophageal varices are found. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: "Recurrent acute pancreatitis" for years, then hematemesis with varices and splenomegaly but "all labs normal" (no liver disease) is the classic picture of left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension. The splenic vein runs along the back of the pancreas; inflammation thromboses it, splenic blood diverts through the short gastric veins and produces varices (classically gastric fundal) while the portal vein and liver are normal. Hyperlipidemia here is just the cause of the pancreatitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Angiodysplasia causes painless GI bleeding, typically in the elderly (often with aortic stenosis or CKD), but it does not produce varices or splenomegaly.
B. An arteriovenous shunt into the portal system (e.g. after trauma or liver biopsy) raises pressure in the whole portal system; nothing in this history suggests it, and pancreatitis points to splenic vein thrombosis instead.
D. Splenic artery aneurysm can complicate pancreatitis and may rupture with sudden hemorrhage, but it is an arterial lesion and does not create varices.
key_concept:
Pancreatitis + varices + splenomegaly + normal liver = splenic vein thrombosis (sinistral portal hypertension).
  • Splenic vein lies on the posterior pancreas, so pancreatitis or pancreatic tumour can thrombose it
  • Collaterals via short gastric veins give isolated gastric (fundal) varices
  • Portal vein and liver function are normal
  • Definitive treatment: splenectomy (removes the inflow)
  • Portosystemic shunts are not indicated (portal pressure normal)
exam_pearl: Varices with NORMAL liver tests and a pancreatitis history: think splenic vein thrombosis, and the cure is splenectomy, not a shunt.

stem: Post term has respiratory distress and shifted to NICU. X-ray: patchy, bilateral infiltrates, hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms, increased AP diameter, pneumomediastinum. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: A post-term baby with respiratory distress whose X-ray shows patchy bilateral infiltrates with hyperinflation, flattened diaphragms and an air leak (pneumomediastinum) has meconium aspiration syndrome. Meconium causes patchy atelectasis and ball-valve airway obstruction, giving air trapping and air leaks; post-maturity is the main risk factor.
why_wrong_block: A. TTN is a term (usually CS) baby with mild, self-resolving tachypnoea and perihilar streaks with fluid in the fissures on X-ray; patchy infiltrates with air leak in a post-term baby admitted to NICU point to meconium aspiration instead.
key_concept:
Neonatal distress: gestation plus X-ray picks the diagnosis.
  • Preterm (or term with maternal diabetes): RDS, ground-glass reticulogranular pattern, low volumes
  • Term CS: TTN, perihilar streaks, fluid in fissures, resolves
  • Post-term, meconium-stained liquor: MAS, patchy infiltrates, hyperinflation, air leaks
exam_pearl: Post-term + patchy infiltrates + hyperinflation or pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum = meconium aspiration.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other recall (screenshot): 'A newborn with RD on X-ray: hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm and pneumomediastinum' A-RDS B-MAS C-TE fistula D-TTN. Compiler: Poor recall, both A & D are correct; however if he is pre-term (or term with C-section + maternal diabetes) -> RDS; post-term -> MAS.

stem: Newborn of mother known case of GDM was in distress, born through CS around 37-39 weeks, found to have pneumomediastinum and increased AP diameter with flattened diaphragm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: This recall's key is RDS because of the risk-factor pattern: a mother with GDM (fetal hyperinsulinaemia delays surfactant maturation) and delivery by CS around early term, so surfactant deficiency can occur even near term. Meconium aspiration is not offered, and air leak (pneumomediastinum) is a recognised complication of RDS, especially once ventilated.
why_wrong_block:
A. TTN is the classic term CS baby with mild, self-limiting tachypnoea and fluid in the fissures; here maternal diabetes, which delays lung maturity, is the clue the key uses to choose RDS over TTN.
C. Tracheoesophageal fistula presents with frothy secretions, choking and cyanosis with feeds and failure to pass a nasogastric tube (coiled on X-ray), not with distress plus hyperinflation at birth.
key_concept:
Risk factor sorts the neonatal distress question.
  • Preterm, or early-term with maternal diabetes (especially by CS): RDS (surfactant deficiency)
  • Term CS without other risk: TTN
  • Post-term: meconium aspiration syndrome
  • RDS X-ray: ground-glass, air bronchograms, low lung volumes
  • TTN X-ray: perihilar streaks, fissural fluid, may be hyperinflated
exam_pearl: Maternal diabetes is the clue examiners use to turn a near-term CS baby from TTN into RDS.
compiler_note: Compiler note: No meconium aspiration syndrome in choices. Compiler: pre-term (or term with C-section + maternal diabetes) -> RDS; post-term -> MAS.

stem: 6-week-old infant, currently below the 3rd percentile for weight, presents with stridor that worsens when supine and improves when prone. The infant also experiences apneic episodes and abnormal breathing sounds. Clinical suspicion is high for laryngomalacia. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: stridor that worsens when supine and improves when prone
why_right: Positional stridor that is worse supine and better prone fits laryngomalacia, which is usually self-limiting. But this infant has red flags of severe disease: weight "below the 3rd percentile" (failure to thrive) and "apneic episodes". Severe laryngomalacia needs ENT referral for laryngoscopy to confirm the diagnosis and assess for surgery (supraglottoplasty), so referral is the most appropriate next step.
why_wrong_block:
B. Reassure the parents: right for mild laryngomalacia with normal growth and no apnea, which resolves by 1 to 2 years. Failure to thrive and apnea rule out simple reassurance here.
C. Start bronchodilators: laryngomalacia is a structural floppiness of the supraglottic larynx, not bronchospasm, so bronchodilators do nothing. They suit wheeze from asthma, not inspiratory stridor.
D. Order a chest X-ray: does not show the larynx or confirm laryngomalacia. Diagnosis is by direct laryngoscopy, done by ENT.
key_concept:
Laryngomalacia: worse supine, better prone; severity decides management.
  • Mild (normal growth, no apnea): reassure, resolves by 1 to 2 years
  • Severe (failure to thrive, apnea, cyanosis, feeding difficulty): refer ENT
  • Diagnosis: laryngoscopy
  • Tracheomalacia: noise disappears supine; diagnosed by bronchoscopy
exam_pearl: Same positional stridor: normal growth = reassure; failure to thrive or apnea = refer ENT.

stem: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the clinic by her mother, who is concerned about potential exposure to gastroenteritis after the infant's older sister was diagnosed several days ago. The infant is currently well-appearing and up to date on vaccinations. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?
OptD: Reassure the mother and monitor for symptoms
highlight_terms_source: well-appearing and up to date on vaccinations
why_right: The infant is "well-appearing" and "up to date on vaccinations", so at 3 months she has already had her first rotavirus dose (given at 2 months). There is no post-exposure prophylaxis for viral gastroenteritis, so the correct advice is reassurance and watching for symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea and signs of dehydration, with good hand hygiene at home.
why_wrong_block:
A. Encourage increased free water intake: a 3-month-old should get breast milk or formula only; extra free water risks hyponatremia. If diarrhea develops, oral rehydration solution is used, not plain water.
B. Administer the rotavirus vaccine: she is already up to date, and rotavirus vaccine is given on schedule, not as post-exposure prophylaxis. It would be right only for a missed scheduled dose within the age window.
C. Discontinue fruit juice at dinner: a 3-month-old should not be taking juice at all, and stopping juice does not prevent infection. Juice restriction matters for toddler's diarrhea, not exposure.
key_concept:
Well infant exposed to gastroenteritis: reassure and monitor.
  • No post-exposure prophylaxis for viral gastroenteritis
  • Rotavirus is the only common viral cause with a vaccine; given on schedule from 2 months
  • If symptoms start: oral rehydration solution and continued feeding
  • Under 6 months: no free water or juice
exam_pearl: "Up to date on vaccinations" means rotavirus is already given; do not re-vaccinate after exposure.

stem: A child presents with recurrent infections including pneumonia, upper respiratory tract infections, and his mother confirmed he had episodes of diarrhea. Which of the following investigations is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: recurrent infections including pneumonia, upper respiratory tract infections
why_right: Recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections ("pneumonia, upper respiratory tract infections") plus chronic "diarrhea" are the typical pattern of a humoral (antibody) immunodeficiency, such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia, CVID or IgA deficiency (often with Giardia diarrhea). The first screening test for suspected antibody deficiency is serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM).
why_wrong_block:
A. Check C1 inhibitor levels: tests for hereditary angioedema (recurrent non-itchy swelling, abdominal attacks), not recurrent infections.
B. Hemolytic complement (CH50): screens for complement deficiency, classically recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal) infections or lupus-like disease. It is a second-line test once immunoglobulins are normal, not the first screen for sinopulmonary infections with diarrhea.
C. Thrombocytopenia: a finding, not an investigation. Low platelets with eczema and infections would point to Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, which is not described here.
key_concept:
Match infection pattern to the immune arm and its first test.
  • Recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections ± diarrhea: antibody defect → serum immunoglobulins
  • Recurrent Neisseria: complement → CH50
  • Fungal, viral, opportunistic: T-cell defect → lymphocyte count / subsets
  • Catalase-positive abscesses: phagocyte defect (CGD) → neutrophil function test
  • Recurrent swelling without urticaria: C1 inhibitor
exam_pearl: Sinopulmonary infections plus Giardia-type diarrhea = antibody deficiency; start with immunoglobulin levels.

stem: 5 year Down syndrome, came with diarrhea and irritability.
why_right: Down syndrome carries a higher risk of autoimmune thyroid disease, including Graves hyperthyroidism as well as hypothyroidism. "Diarrhea and irritability" are typical hyperthyroid features (increased gut motility, restlessness), so thyroid function tests are the right investigation. Thyroid screening is also part of routine Down syndrome follow-up.
why_wrong_block: B. US Abdomen: suits a structural or surgical cause (mass, intussusception, obstruction), but there is no pain, mass or vomiting here. Irritability with diarrhea points to a systemic, endocrine cause.
key_concept:
Down syndrome conditions to screen for when new symptoms appear:
  • Thyroid disease (congenital hypothyroidism, later Hashimoto or Graves): TFTs
  • Celiac disease: tTG-IgA with total IgA
  • Duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung disease (neonatal)
  • AVSD (most common heart defect)
  • Leukemia; atlantoaxial instability
exam_pearl: Diarrhea in Down syndrome has two main suspects: hyperthyroidism (irritable, restless) and celiac disease (poor growth, bloating); check which test the options offer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: He doesn't remember if celiac was present or not. Not sure if presence of celiac would change the answer. Diarrhea + mood changes (irritability) = think of HYPER-thyroidism. Does Down predispose to hyperthyroidism? (Know hypo, not sure of hyper; did not search for it.)

stem: A 30-year-old underwent a laparoscopic appendectomy 2 weeks ago (see report). Histology: carcinoid tumor at the tip of the appendix measuring 0.5 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptD: CT scan of chest abdomen and pelvis
highlight_terms_source: carcinoid tumor at the tip of the appendix
why_right: An appendiceal carcinoid (neuroendocrine tumour) that is small ("0.5 cm", well under 2 cm) and at the "tip" of the appendix, with no mesoappendix or nodal involvement, is cured by the appendectomy already done. Its metastatic risk is negligible, so no further surgery, imaging or endoscopy is needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colonoscopy is for synchronous colonic pathology, e.g. after an appendiceal mass or abscess treated conservatively in an older patient; a small tip carcinoid does not require it.
C. Right hemicolectomy is reserved for carcinoid >2 cm, at the base of the appendix, or with mesoappendix or lymph node invasion (and for appendiceal adenocarcinoma).
D. Staging CT is used for larger or invasive tumours or adenocarcinoma; a 0.5 cm tip lesion does not need staging.
key_concept:
Appendiceal carcinoid: size, site and invasion decide.
  • <2 cm, at tip, no mesoappendix/node invasion: appendectomy alone, observe
  • >2 cm, OR at base, OR mesoappendix/node invasion: right hemicolectomy
  • Appendiceal adenocarcinoma: right hemicolectomy
exam_pearl: Same tumour at the BASE of the appendix (or >2 cm) flips the answer to right hemicolectomy.

stem: 33-year-old female patient presented with anal fistula; on examination: external opening at 7 o'clock; you are planning for fistulotomy. Where is the most likely site of internal opening?
why_right: By Goodsall's rule, draw a transverse line across the anus (3 to 9 o'clock). An external opening at "7 o'clock" lies posterior to that line, and posterior openings follow a curved tract to an internal opening in the posterior midline (6 o'clock). Knowing the internal opening is essential before fistulotomy so the whole tract is laid open.
why_wrong_block:
B. The anterior midline is not where this tract goes; anterior external openings (in front of the 3 to 9 line) track radially in a straight line to the nearest crypt, not to 12 o'clock specifically.
C. A lateral internal opening is not predicted by Goodsall's rule; anterior openings drain straight radially and posterior openings curve to the posterior midline.
D. A tract with no internal opening is a sinus, not a fistula; the stem states anal fistula, which by definition connects the anal canal to the skin.
key_concept:
Goodsall's rule (transverse line through 3 and 9 o'clock).
  • External opening POSTERIOR to the line: curved tract to posterior midline (6 o'clock)
  • External opening ANTERIOR to the line: straight radial tract to nearest crypt
  • Exception: anterior openings far from the anal verge (>3 cm) may still curve to the posterior midline
  • Low simple fistula: fistulotomy; high or complex: MRI then seton or sphincter-sparing surgery
exam_pearl: Any opening between 3 and 9 o'clock on the back half points to 6 o'clock midline, whatever its exact hour.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Highlight is on the 'Q:' restatement (A. Left lateral, B. Midline anterior, C. Midline posterior, D. Straight lateral) where C. Midline posterior is highlighted. 6 o'clock -> posterior; 12 o'clock -> anterior (Goodsall rule).

stem: 8 years old boy presented with focal pain on his left leg that is increasing in intensity, associated with local warmth and tenderness and subjective fever. He has a history of fall with wound. What is the radiological investigation for the leg?
highlight_terms_source: focal pain on his left leg
local warmth and tenderness and subjective fever
why_right: Increasing focal pain with "local warmth and tenderness" and fever after a fall with a wound in a child suggests acute osteomyelitis. This recall's key is MRI because it is the most sensitive and specific imaging for osteomyelitis: it shows marrow edema within days and detects subperiosteal abscess, while plain films stay normal for about the first 10 to 14 days.
why_wrong_block:
A. X ray: usually done first as a baseline to exclude fracture or foreign body, but early osteomyelitis looks normal on X-ray; bone changes appear only after 1 to 2 weeks. It is the answer if the question asks for the initial study.
C. CT scan: shows cortical bone and sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis but is poor for early marrow changes and exposes the child to radiation.
D. Nuclear scan: sensitive bone scan useful when the site is unclear or multifocal, or when MRI is unavailable; less specific than MRI and gives no anatomy of abscesses.
key_concept:
Imaging in pediatric acute osteomyelitis:
  • X-ray: first-line baseline, normal early
  • MRI: investigation of choice (most sensitive and specific)
  • Bone scan: site unclear or multifocal, MRI unavailable
  • Ultrasound: joint effusion or subperiosteal collection
  • Diagnosis confirmed by blood culture or bone aspirate
exam_pearl: "Initial" imaging = X-ray; "best" or "most sensitive" imaging = MRI.

stem: 6 y old boy presents with convulsions, pallor, hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, Hb and plt low, WBCs 25. What is the line of management for his CNS, should it be involved?
why_right: Pallor, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, low Hb and platelets with a high WBC in a 6-year-old is acute leukemia (most likely ALL), and "convulsions" raise concern for CNS involvement. Most systemic chemotherapy does not cross the blood-brain barrier well, so CNS leukemia is treated (and prevented) with intrathecal chemotherapy, typically methotrexate, given into the CSF.
why_wrong_block:
A. Systemic chemotherapy: the backbone treatment for the leukemia overall, but standard IV drugs reach the CSF poorly, so on its own it does not control CNS disease.
C. Anticonvulsant: controls the seizures symptomatically but does not treat the leukemic infiltration that is causing them.
D. Ventriculopleural shunt: a CSF diversion for hydrocephalus; it does not treat CNS leukemia and is not part of its management.
key_concept:
Childhood ALL and the CNS:
  • Features: pallor, bleeding, infections, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy
  • Diagnosis: bone marrow aspiration
  • CNS is a sanctuary site because of the blood-brain barrier
  • CNS prophylaxis and treatment: intrathecal chemotherapy (methotrexate)
  • Cranial irradiation is reserved for selected high-risk cases
exam_pearl: CNS is a sanctuary site in ALL: the treatment goes into the CSF (intrathecal), not just the vein.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Explanation linked externally (Telegram).

stem: A 34-year-old woman with progressive dysphagia diagnosed as a case of achalasia. She has no medical problem and not on any medications. She is clinically unremarkable (see lab results): RBC 4, Hb 10, platelets 455, WBC 9, urea 5, creatinine 98. Which of the following is the best treatment option?
why_right: This is a young ("34-year-old"), otherwise healthy woman with achalasia, so she should get definitive therapy. Heller myotomy is first line but is not offered; pneumatic dilatation is the other definitive, durable treatment and is the best listed choice. The mild labs (Hb 10, platelets 455) are distractors and do not contraindicate dilatation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fundoplication alone is an anti-reflux operation for GERD; in achalasia it is only added to a Heller myotomy, and on its own it would worsen the outflow obstruction.
C. Oral nitrates (isosorbide dinitrate) give weak, short-lived LES relaxation and are reserved for patients unfit for dilatation or surgery.
D. Botulinum toxin gives temporary relief and is reserved for elderly or high-risk patients unfit for definitive treatment, not a fit 34-year-old.
key_concept:
Achalasia treatment by fitness.
  • Fit patient: Heller myotomy (with partial fundoplication) first line
  • Pneumatic dilatation: other definitive option, chosen when myotomy is not offered
  • Unfit/elderly/high risk: botulinum toxin injection
  • Drugs (nitrates, calcium channel blockers): weakest, bridging or unfit patients
exam_pearl: Young and fit = definitive therapy (myotomy, or dilatation if myotomy is absent); Botox is the answer only when the patient is old or unfit.

stem: X ray I think it was boot shape heart of 6 days old child with sx of cyanosis, ask abt most important management at this age I remember 2
why_right: A "boot shape heart" with cyanosis is Tetralogy of Fallot. In a cyanotic "6 days old" newborn, pulmonary blood flow may depend on the ductus arteriosus, which is closing in the first days of life. Prostaglandin E1 keeps the duct open and maintains pulmonary flow until definitive repair, so it is the most important management at this age.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cardiac catheterization: TOF is diagnosed by echocardiography; catheterization is not needed for diagnosis and is not the urgent step in a cyanotic neonate. It has a role in selected anatomy or interventions later.
C. Elective surgical repair: this is the definitive treatment, usually at 3 to 6 months of age, but it is not the immediate step for a cyanotic 6-day-old whose ductus is closing.
key_concept:
Cyanotic newborn with suspected duct-dependent CHD: start PGE1 first.
  • TOF CXR: boot shaped heart, reduced pulmonary markings
  • TOF confirmatory test: echocardiography
  • TOF definitive repair: 3 to 6 months
  • Tet spell: knee to chest, oxygen, morphine, IV fluids, beta blocker
  • TGA CXR: egg on a string; also PGE1 first
exam_pearl: Newborn cyanotic CHD = PGE1 first; elective repair is the answer only when asked for definitive treatment.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Image caption: Boot shaped heart = TOF.

stem: A 4 month old baby with cough, running nose, nasal flaring, increase work of breathing with no fever, on examination expiratory wheeze in all lower lung zones and suprasternal retraction. What is the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: expiratory wheeze in all lower lung zones
why_right: A "4 month old" with upper airway symptoms (cough, "running nose") followed by lower airway signs (diffuse "expiratory wheeze", nasal flaring, retractions) is the classic picture of bronchiolitis, usually from RSV. Low grade or absent fever fits, and it is a clinical diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pneumonia: usually brings fever, focal crackles or reduced breath sounds and focal consolidation, not diffuse wheeze in all lung zones.
C. Bronchial asthma: needs recurrent episodes and is not diagnosed in a 4-month-old with a first wheezy illness after a cold; it suits an older child with recurrent wheeze and atopy.
D. Viral croup: an upper airway illness of 6 months to 3 years with barking cough and inspiratory stridor, not expiratory wheeze.
key_concept:
Infant wheeze after a cold = bronchiolitis.
  • Age under 2 years (peak under 1 year); RSV most common
  • URTI (coryza, cough) then LRTI (wheeze, crackles, retractions)
  • Clinical diagnosis; CXR not routine
  • Treatment supportive: oxygen and hydration
  • Croup: barking cough + inspiratory stridor; asthma: recurrent wheeze in older child
exam_pearl: Expiratory wheeze = lower airway (bronchiolitis); inspiratory stridor with barking cough = upper airway (croup).

stem: Woman with known chronic hepatitis B infection delivers a healthy newborn. The infant receives hepatitis B vaccine shortly after birth. What to give?
OptB: Second dose of hepatitis B vaccine
why_right: A baby born to a mother with "chronic hepatitis B" (HBsAg-positive) needs both active and passive immunization. The vaccine has already been given, so the missing piece is hepatitis B immunoglobulin, ideally within 12 hours of birth, to sharply reduce vertical transmission.
why_wrong_block: B. Second dose of hepatitis B vaccine: the series continues on schedule at 1 to 2 months, not immediately. It does not replace HBIG, which gives the immediate passive protection the vaccine alone cannot.
key_concept:
Newborn of HBsAg-positive mother:
  • Hepatitis B vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours of birth
  • Complete the vaccine series on schedule
  • Test the infant for HBsAg and anti-HBs after the series
  • Breastfeeding is not contraindicated
exam_pearl: Mother HBsAg-positive: vaccine alone is not enough; add HBIG within 12 hours.

stem: A newborn presents with ambiguous genitalia and clitoromegaly. Laboratory findings show hyponatremia, hyperkalemia. The 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is elevated. What is the most appropriate initial/next management?
why_right: Ambiguous genitalia with clitoromegaly, raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone, "hyponatremia, hyperkalemia" is salt-wasting CAH from 21-hydroxylase deficiency. The electrolyte picture signals an adrenal crisis that can lead to shock, so the most appropriate initial management is IV hydrocortisone with IV fluid (saline) resuscitation, adding glucose if hypoglycemic.
why_wrong_block: A. Karyotyping & ultrasound: needed to confirm genetic sex and internal anatomy in ambiguous genitalia, but they do not treat a life-threatening salt-wasting crisis. They are the answer for a stable baby with ambiguous genitalia and normal electrolytes.
key_concept:
Salt-wasting CAH (21-hydroxylase deficiency):
  • Girls: ambiguous genitalia; boys: may present only with crisis at 1 to 3 weeks
  • Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, acidosis, hypoglycemia, shock
  • Diagnosis: raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone
  • Acute: IV hydrocortisone + saline (+ glucose if low)
  • Long term: hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone; autosomal recessive
exam_pearl: Abnormal electrolytes turn "workup" into "resuscitate": stabilize first, karyotype later.

stem: Child with features of ADHD ( talkative and interrupt others ) The Q was about what to do to prevent the progression of this symptom?
OptC: restrict or limit the screen time
key_concept:
ADHD management depends on age.
  • Under 6 years: parent training in behaviour management first
  • 6 years and older: stimulant medication plus behavioural therapy and school support
  • Core techniques: positive reinforcement, planned ignoring, consistent limits, time out
exam_pearl: For a child with ADHD features and a "what to do" lead in, the parent based behavioural programme usually beats general lifestyle advice.

stem: 70 years old male complain of severe chest pain and change in voice after 8 hours of pneumatic dilatation of esophageal stricture What is the cause ?
why_right: Severe chest pain hours after "pneumatic dilatation of esophageal stricture" is iatrogenic esophageal perforation until proven otherwise; endoscopic instrumentation is the commonest cause of esophageal perforation. The "change in voice" fits air tracking into the neck and mediastinum (subcutaneous/mediastinal emphysema). Work-up is neck and chest X-ray, then a water-soluble contrast study or CT with oral contrast, with NPO, IV antibiotics and resuscitation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aspiration after endoscopy presents with cough, dyspnea, fever and hypoxia with lung infiltrates, not severe chest pain with voice change.
B. Bleeding after dilatation shows as hematemesis or melena and hemodynamic change, not severe retrosternal pain and voice change.
D. MI should be excluded with an ECG in a 70-year-old with chest pain, but the clear link to esophageal instrumentation plus voice change points to perforation.
key_concept:
Chest pain after esophageal instrumentation = perforation.
  • Clues: retrosternal pain, fever, tachycardia, subcutaneous emphysema/crepitus, Hamman crunch
  • Step 1: neck and chest X-ray (pneumomediastinum, effusion, surgical emphysema)
  • Confirm: water-soluble contrast esophagram, or CT with oral contrast if unstable
  • Initial care: ABC, NPO, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV PPI, analgesia
  • Large free leak: surgical repair; small contained, stable: nonoperative or endoscopic
exam_pearl: Post-dilatation or post-endoscopy chest pain is perforation, not cardiac, unless proven otherwise.

stem: Female PT with RLQ pain and no Fever, WBC within normal range, what to do?
OptB: discharge and tell them to return if the pain worsening
why_right: RLQ pain with "no fever" and a "normal WBC" is an equivocal picture: appendicitis is not excluded (early appendicitis can have normal labs), and in a woman ovarian and other pelvic causes remain possible. With only these two choices, the safe answer is active observation: admit, repeat clinical examination and labs (about 6 hours later) and image as needed. Note the recall says imaging and a pregnancy test were not among the options.
why_wrong_block: B. Discharge with return advice is suitable only once a serious cause has been reasonably excluded (low-risk score, reassuring exam and work-up); with unexplained RLQ pain and no imaging, sending her home risks missing appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy or torsion.
key_concept:
Equivocal RLQ pain: observe and reassess rather than discharge.
  • Normal WBC and no fever do not exclude early appendicitis
  • Woman of reproductive age: pregnancy test always (ectopic)
  • Imaging: CT best in non-pregnant adults, US in pregnancy and children
  • Pelvic differentials: ovarian torsion, ruptured cyst, PID, ectopic
  • Serial examination converts an equivocal case into a clear one
exam_pearl: When the picture is unclear, admitting for serial examination beats discharge; discharge only after the dangerous causes are excluded.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Note in recall: no US, no pregnancy test, no CT (among options).

stem: Female PT with RLQ pain and no Fever, primary investigation:
why_right: In a "female" with RLQ pain the first bedside investigations must cover the three big groups: CBC (inflammation, anemia from bleeding), pregnancy test (ectopic pregnancy, and it must be known before any CT radiation) and urinalysis (UTI, pyelonephritis, ureteric stone with hematuria). Only option C covers all three; imaging follows these results.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ultrasound is the usual next imaging (pelvic organs, appendix, especially if pregnant), but it comes after the basic labs, above all the pregnancy test, which changes what imaging and differential you pursue.
B. CBC alone misses the two key differentials in a woman with RLQ pain: pregnancy (ectopic) and urinary causes.
D. RFT and LFT are not targeted at RLQ pain causes and omit the pregnancy test and urinalysis.
key_concept:
Female with lower abdominal pain: CBC + pregnancy test + urinalysis first.
  • Pregnancy test: ectopic pregnancy and radiation safety before CT
  • Urinalysis: UTI, pyelonephritis, renal stone (hematuria)
  • CBC: leukocytosis, anemia
  • Then imaging: US in pregnancy or for pelvic causes; CT best for appendicitis in non-pregnant adults
exam_pearl: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain: pregnancy test before imaging.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Separate 'Q:' recall under 1581 with a different lead-in and options.

stem: A 5-year-old girl's mother noticed two episodes of night bedwetting, starting after the birth of her sister. She remains dry in the evening.
highlight_terms_source: after the birth of her sister
why_right: This is secondary enuresis in a 5-year-old: she was previously dry, wetting started after a clear stressor ("after the birth of her sister") and there have been only two episodes. A short, stress-related regression like this is managed first with reassurance and simple behavioural measures, of which restricting evening fluids (plus voiding before bed and avoiding blame) is the practical first step.
why_wrong_block: A. Psychiatric evaluation is excessive for two wetting episodes clearly linked to a new sibling; it is considered only if there are persistent behavioural or emotional problems, or signs of abuse or major family stress.
key_concept:
Enuresis: rule out organic causes, then behavioural measures first.
  • Primary: never dry for 6 months; usually maturational, often familial
  • Secondary: wetting after a dry period; look for stressor, UTI, diabetes, constipation
  • Simple check: urinalysis (glucose, infection)
  • First line: reassurance, evening fluid limit, void before bed, reward chart
  • Persistent cases: enuresis alarm (most effective long term), desmopressin for short-term control
exam_pearl: New sibling + brief regression = behavioural measures, not a psychiatry referral; polyuria, daytime wetting or dysuria would instead demand urinalysis and work-up.

stem: A patient presents after trauma with: GCS = 14, Neurological weakness, CT scan shows intracranial hematoma. Blood pressure is low. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: The decisive clue is "blood pressure is low" in a head-injured patient. Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP minus ICP, so hypotension causes secondary brain injury and must be corrected first; ATLS order puts Circulation before Disability. With "GCS = 14" the airway is protected (no intubation needed), so the initial step is IV fluid resuscitation, followed by neurosurgery for the hematoma with weakness once the patient is resuscitated.
why_wrong_block:
A. Corticosteroids are not used in traumatic brain injury; they increased mortality in head injury trials. Steroids belong to vasogenic edema around tumours, not trauma.
C. Surgical evacuation is the definitive treatment for a hematoma with focal weakness, and would be the answer if the patient were normotensive; but hypotension must be corrected first.
D. Observation is for a small hematoma with no deficit in a stable patient; this patient has a focal deficit and shock.
key_concept:
Head injury + hypotension: fix C before D.
  • CPP = MAP minus ICP; hypotension worsens brain injury
  • GCS 8 or less: intubate first (airway)
  • Hypotensive: IV fluids, and search for another bleeding source
  • Stable with hematoma and focal deficit: urgent neurosurgical evacuation
  • Steroids: no role in TBI
exam_pearl: Same hematoma with normal BP flips the answer to neurosurgery; with GCS 8 or less it flips to intubation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: In patients with TBI, hypotension should be corrected immediately to maintain cerebral perfusion; fluid resuscitation is the first step. Comment (December File p1039): patient has weakness but is hypotensive, so fix ABC as initial; if GCS 8 or coma, intubation is initial; otherwise initial for weakness would still be surgery. Athar: Agree.

stem: Young male (around 20) Pt presented after he has a BLUNT abdominal trauma CT: there was Extravasation around the left kidney What are most appropriate step in management?
key_concept:
Blunt renal trauma: stability first, then CT findings.
  • Unstable despite resuscitation: surgery (exploration, nephrectomy if unreconstructable)
  • Stable, most grades: nonoperative, observe and repeat CT
  • Stable with active contrast extravasation, pseudoaneurysm or AV fistula: angioembolization
  • Urinary extravasation: observe, repeat CT; stent or nephrostomy if it persists
  • Renal pedicle avulsion: surgery
exam_pearl: "Extravasation" alone is not enough: contrast blush in a stable patient = angioembolization; urine leak = observe; unstable = theatre.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No option marked on the numbered recall. Compiler: answer depends on URINARY vs CONTRAST/BLOOD extravasation; we also need to know option D. Blunt renal trauma: unstable -> surgery; stable -> by CT: grade 1-4 observe and repeat CT; grade 5 shattered kidney observe if stable; renal pedicle injury or grade 4-5 vascular -> surgery. Urinary extravasation -> observe and repeat CT (JJ stent or nephrostomy if persists); contrast extravasation -> observe +/- angio.
