stem: 40-something-year-old woman presents after blunt abdominal trauma. She is initially hypotensive despite resuscitation, but her blood pressure is now 100/80 mmHg. A CT scan shows contrast extravasation near the left kidney with a perirenal hematoma. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: contrast extravasation near the left kidney
why_right: She was hypotensive but has now responded to resuscitation ("BP is now 100/80"), so she is stable enough to stay out of theatre. CT shows active contrast extravasation with a perirenal hematoma, meaning an arterial bleed that will not reliably stop on its own. In a stable or responding patient with blunt renal injury and active extravasation, angioembolization stops the bleeding while preserving the kidney.
why_wrong_block:
A. Emergent nephrectomy is for the patient who stays unstable despite resuscitation (non responder) or has an expanding or pulsatile hematoma at laparotomy; she has responded, so a kidney sparing option comes first.
B. Repeat CT after 6 months ignores an active bleed now; delayed imaging is for follow up of a healed injury, not acute management.
D. Foley catheter and monitoring is conservative care for a stable, low grade renal injury with no active extravasation; contrast blush here means ongoing arterial bleeding.
key_concept:
Blunt renal trauma: decide by hemodynamics first, then by active bleeding on CT.
  • Stable, no extravasation: non operative (bed rest, monitoring, serial Hb).
  • Stable or transient responder with contrast extravasation: angioembolization.
  • Persistently unstable: operative exploration, nephrectomy if kidney not salvageable.
  • Unstable patients do not go to CT; they go to FAST then laparotomy.
exam_pearl: Contrast blush in a now stable patient = angioembolization; if the BP never recovers, the answer flips to surgery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant under 1589; options continue on p405 where C is highlighted. Compiler: contrast extravasation -> observe +/- angio; unstable -> surgery.

stem: Young male ( around 20) Pt presented after he has a BLUNT abdominal trauma CT : there was CONTRAST Extravasation around the left kidney I THINK Patient Was UNSTABLE What are most appropriate step in management ?
key_concept:
Blunt renal trauma: hemodynamics decide.
  • Stable, no blush: observe (fluids, bed rest, serial Hb).
  • Stable or responder with blush: angioembolization.
  • Persistently unstable: surgery (exploration, nephrectomy if not salvageable).
  • A truly unstable patient should not be in the CT scanner; instability is managed in theatre.

stem: Pediatric patient presented in ER with fever and barky cough a long senario but he was in distress Bp was 80/60, Oxygen was 80% What is the appropriate initial management?
OptC: Some type of intubation in the OR
key_concept:
Barky cough + distress: grade severity, then treat the airway.
  • Mild croup (no stridor at rest): single dose dexamethasone
  • Moderate/severe (stridor at rest, retractions): nebulized epinephrine + steroid + oxygen
  • Impending failure (hypoxia, fatigue, altered consciousness): secure airway
  • Toxic, high fever, drooling, tripod: epiglottitis, prepare for intubation + 3rd generation cephalosporin
  • Toxic with barky cough not responding to epinephrine: bacterial tracheitis
exam_pearl: SpO2 80% is never plain mild croup: oxygen and airway assessment come first, then look for severe croup versus a bacterial airway infection.

stem: 2 y Pediatric patient presented in ER with low grade fever and (brassy cough!) not barky. What is the appropriate initial management?
why_right: A 2-year-old with low grade fever and a croupy cough, with no stridor at rest and no hypoxia mentioned, has mild croup. Dexamethasone is the primary treatment of croup at every severity, and for mild disease a single dose of dexamethasone alone is the appropriate initial management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cool humidified air is a traditional home measure without proven benefit; it does not replace a steroid dose.
B. Prednisolone is an acceptable alternative steroid, but dexamethasone is preferred because it is longer acting, given once and best supported by evidence.
D. Racemic epinephrine is reserved for moderate to severe croup (stridor at rest, retractions, distress); it acts fast but briefly and is not needed in mild croup.
key_concept:
Croup treatment follows severity.
  • Cause: parainfluenza virus; clinical diagnosis (steeple sign if X-ray done)
  • Mild: dexamethasone single dose, home
  • Moderate/severe: nebulized epinephrine + dexamethasone, observe for rebound
  • Epinephrine may be repeated if no response
  • No antibiotics, antihistamines or bronchodilators
exam_pearl: Stridor at rest or retractions flips the answer to racemic epinephrine (plus steroid); without them, steroid alone.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: 'Q: Mild symptoms clear question?' (typed options Dexa 0.6 / Prednisone / Racemic epinephrine). Screenshot marks D racemic epinephrine, but compiler: now we have the full recall; stridor not mentioned, hypoxia not mentioned, mild retractions, stem INITIAL. This is MILD croup, epinephrine is NOT needed; answer is Dexa (all are steroids). Another version (2 y male, low grade fever, brassy cough and inspiratory stridor, most appropriate management; humidified air / prednisone 2.5 / dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg / racemic epinephrine): answer to this specific recall remains C.

stem: Patient KCO Rt inguinal hernia for 6 years (don't remember age) came complaining of irreducible swelling, pain in Rt inguinal region.
OptD: I don't remember 4th option maybe observe?
why_right: A long standing right inguinal hernia that has become irreducible and painful is an incarcerated hernia at risk of obstruction and strangulation, so it needs urgent operative exploration rather than further imaging or waiting. The recall keys this as exploratory laparotomy, and the other version of the question (obstruction with guarding and rigidity) points the same way: signs of compromised bowel mean surgery now.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diagnostic laparoscopy is for when the diagnosis is unclear (for example abdominal pain after surgery); here the diagnosis is clinically obvious and the hernia needs definitive repair.
C. Double contrast pelvic CT delays surgery in a clinically diagnosed painful irreducible hernia; imaging is for doubtful cases or an occult hernia.
D. Observation is never right for a painful irreducible hernia, because strangulated bowel can become gangrenous within hours.
key_concept:
Groin hernia states guide urgency.
  • Reducible: elective mesh repair.
  • Irreducible, painful: urgent surgery.
  • Obstructed (vomiting, distension): urgent surgery after resuscitation.
  • Strangulated (tense, very tender, red skin, systemic signs): emergency surgery, resect nonviable bowel.
exam_pearl: Painful irreducible hernia = operate now; scans and observation are the traps.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): intestinal obstruction, incarcerated hernia with guarding and rigidity, I think management is laparotomy? Options: A. Laparoscopy, B. Exploratory surgery for the hernia.

stem: 45 years old patient, came with history reducible hernia in inguinal area it pop out every two days with mild pain and he can manual reducible it by his finger, then he suddenly developed severe constant pain in early morning in that area and came to hospital, on examination of the inguinal area and scrotum examination and he is free from both them and pain is disappear, Now just have persistent nausea and vomiting, what is the next step ?
why_right: After "sudden severe constant pain" in a known hernia, the groin and scrotum are now empty and the pain has gone, yet he has persistent nausea and vomiting. This raises concern that a strangulated or obstructed segment was reduced into the abdomen (reduction en masse or reduced ischemic bowel), so the next step is CT abdomen and pelvis to look for obstruction or bowel ischemia before deciding on surgery.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hernia repair today after 2 hours treats the groin defect but does not address what is happening inside the abdomen; operative planning should follow imaging of the persistent vomiting.
C. Reassurance and discharge is unsafe because ongoing vomiting after an acute hernia episode can mean obstructed or ischemic bowel.
D. Hernia repair after 2 days fits an uncomplicated reducible hernia once symptoms settle; some recall versions mark this, but it ignores persistent vomiting that still needs explaining.
key_concept:
Hernia that went back in but symptoms persist: image the abdomen.
  • Empty groin + resolved pain + ongoing vomiting: suspect reduced ischemic bowel or reduction en masse.
  • CT abdomen and pelvis shows obstruction, ischemia or free fluid.
  • Positive CT or peritonitis: urgent laparotomy.
  • No symptoms after reduction: elective repair.
exam_pearl: Pain gone but vomiting persists after a hernia reduces = do not discharge; image for hidden obstruction.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Option D text in the recall ends with the word 'answer', while the compiler highlights A.
Other marked answers: Recall text: D. Hernia repair after 2 days

stem: Elderly male presents with massive LGIB (no PMHx). Most likely cause?
why_right: An "elderly male" with massive lower GI bleeding and no relevant history most likely has diverticulosis, the commonest cause of painless, large volume hematochezia in older adults. Diverticular bleeding is arterial, starts abruptly, and usually stops spontaneously.
why_wrong_block:
B. Colon cancer causes chronic, low volume blood loss with iron deficiency anemia, change in bowel habit or weight loss, not an acute massive bleed.
C. Angiodysplasia is the other main cause of painless bleeding in the elderly, typically recurrent and slower, and linked to aortic stenosis or CKD; when diverticulosis is also listed, diverticulosis is the more common cause of a massive bleed.
D. Ulcerative colitis gives bloody diarrhea with urgency and tenesmus in younger patients, not an isolated massive bleed in an elderly man.
key_concept:
Massive painless LGIB in the elderly: diverticulosis first.
  • Diverticulosis vs angiodysplasia: diverticulosis.
  • Diverticulitis vs angiodysplasia: angiodysplasia (diverticulitis does not bleed).
  • Chronic occult bleed with anemia or weight loss: colon cancer.
  • Bloody diarrhea with urgency: colitis.
exam_pearl: Diverticulosis bleeds, diverticulitis does not; the "osis" vs "itis" spelling flips the answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Diverticulosis (not diverticulitis). Diverticulosis vs angiodysplasia -> diverticulosis; diverticulitis vs angiodysplasia -> angiodysplasia. Diverticulitis does NOT cause GI bleed.

stem: Child with dry patches in face, scalp and extensor surfaces. Sometimes his cheeks are cracked and red and weepy
highlight_terms_source: dry patches in face, scalp and extensor surfaces
cheeks are cracked and red and weepy
why_right: A child with dry patches on the face, scalp and extensor surfaces has the classic infant and toddler distribution of atopic eczema. Red, cracked, weepy cheeks describe acute eczema with exudation. Dry skin plus this age specific distribution makes atopic dermatitis the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Idiopathic urticaria: transient itchy wheals that come and go within 24 hours and leave normal skin; it does not cause dry, cracked, weeping patches in a fixed distribution.
C. Drug induced dermatitis: needs a new drug exposure and usually gives an acute widespread eruption; right when a rash follows a recently started medication.
D. Unrecalled option: no content to judge; the distribution and dry, weepy skin already point to atopic dermatitis.
key_concept:
Atopic eczema: dry, intensely itchy skin with a distribution that changes with age.
  • Under 6 months: face, head and scalp
  • 6 months to 2 years: extensor surfaces and face
  • 2 to 12 years: flexural creases (antecubital and popliteal fossae)
  • Over 12 years: flexures and perioral region
  • Treatment: emollients, non soap cleansers, topical corticosteroids as the cornerstone
  • Honey colored crusts on eczema: secondary impetigo
exam_pearl: Extensor surfaces plus cheeks means a young child's eczema; flexures mean an older child.

stem: A 9-month-old boy presents to the clinic with skin rash noticed by his parent over the past few weeks. His parents are known to have eczema before. Which of the following is the typical site of eczematous plaques at this age?
why_right: In a 9-month-old with an atopic family history, infantile eczema classically involves the face and head: scalp, cheeks and forehead. From about 6 months extensor surfaces join the face, but of these options the facial/scalp pattern is the typical infant site.
why_wrong_block:
A. The upper back is not a classic site of infant eczema; at this age the face, scalp and extensor surfaces of the limbs are typical, with flexures taking over after 2 years.
B. The diaper area is typically spared in atopic eczema because the skin stays moist; a diaper rash suggests irritant or candidal dermatitis.
C. The dorsum of the feet is not the typical infant site; the face, scalp and extensor surfaces are.
key_concept:
Eczema distribution changes with age.
  • <6 months: face, head, scalp
  • 6 months to 2 years: extensor surfaces and face
  • 2 to 12 years: flexures (antecubital, popliteal)
  • >12 years: flexures and perioral region
  • Treatment: emollients, non-soap cleansers, topical steroids
exam_pearl: Infant eczema spares the diaper area; a rash there points away from atopic dermatitis.

stem: An 8-year-old boy presents to the clinic with skin rash noticed by his parent over the past few weeks. His parents are known to have eczema before. Which of the following is the typical site of eczematous plaques at this age?
why_right: An 8-year-old falls in the childhood (2 to 12 years) phase of atopic eczema, which classically affects the flexural creases, especially the antecubital and popliteal fossae.
why_wrong_block:
A. The upper back is not a characteristic eczema site in childhood.
B. The dorsal feet are not the typical childhood site; dorsal foot dermatitis in a child raises shoe contact dermatitis.
D. Scalp, cheeks and forehead are the infant pattern, not that of a school-age child.
key_concept:
Eczema distribution changes with age.
  • <6 months: face, head, scalp
  • 6 months to 2 years: extensor surfaces and face
  • 2 to 12 years: flexures (antecubital, popliteal)
  • >12 years: flexures and perioral region
exam_pearl: Same stem, different age: infant = face/scalp, child = flexures, adolescent = flexures plus perioral.

stem: A 14-year-old boy presents to the clinic with skin rash noticed by his parent over the past few weeks. His parents are known to have eczema before. Which of the following is the typical site of eczematous plaques at this age?
why_right: This recall's key follows the age table for eczema: after 12 years eczema involves flexural surfaces and the perioral region. For a 14-year-old, the site that distinguishes the adolescent pattern from the 2 to 12 year group is the perioral region.
why_wrong_block:
A. The popliteal fossa is the hallmark site of the 2 to 12 year phase; it can persist at 14, but it does not define the adolescent pattern the key asks for.
C. The antecubital fossa is likewise the hallmark 2 to 12 year flexural site; it is not the site specific to adolescence.
D. Scalp and forehead are the infantile pattern.
key_concept:
Eczema distribution changes with age.
  • <6 months: face, head, scalp
  • 6 months to 2 years: extensor surfaces and face
  • 2 to 12 years: flexures (antecubital, popliteal)
  • >12 years: flexures and perioral region (also face, neck, hands)
exam_pearl: Age pattern: popliteal/antecubital = 2 to 12 years, perioral = adolescent; when the question asks for the age-typical site, pick the age-specific one.

stem: down$ (didn't say down) depressed nasal bridge and Single Palmar Crease.
why_right: A depressed (flat) nasal bridge and single palmar crease are dysmorphic features of Down syndrome. The most common endocrine disorder in trisomy 21 is hypothyroidism (congenital or acquired, mostly autoimmune), which is why these children have repeated thyroid screening.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcaemia is the classic endocrine feature of DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome, not Down syndrome.
C. Hypopituitarism is not a characteristic association of trisomy 21; it goes with midline defects such as septo-optic dysplasia.
D. Hyperthyroidism (Graves) is more frequent in Down syndrome than in the general population but far less common than hypothyroidism.
key_concept:
Down syndrome: recognize the face, then screen the associations.
  • Features: upslanting eyes, epicanthic folds, Brushfield spots, flat nasal bridge, protruding tongue, single palmar crease, hypotonia
  • Heart: endocardial cushion (AVSD) defect most typical
  • Endocrine: hypothyroidism most common
  • Also: duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung, leukaemia, atlantoaxial instability, early Alzheimer
exam_pearl: Hypoparathyroidism is the DiGeorge trap; Down syndrome = hypothyroid.

stem: What signs indicate early decompensated shock?
key_concept:
Stages of shock.
  • Compensated: normal BP, tachycardia, tachypnea, cool peripheries, reduced urine output.
  • Decompensated: hypotension, worsening metabolic acidosis, renal failure (anuria).
  • Irreversible: multiorgan failure, poor response to inotropes.
  • Question asks "earliest sign of shock": tachycardia; asks "sign of decompensation": hypotension first.
exam_pearl: Tachycardia = earliest sign of shock; hypotension = first sign of decompensation.

stem: The most initial sign of decompensated shocked:
why_right: In compensated shock, tachycardia and vasoconstriction hold the blood pressure normal; once these mechanisms fail, hypotension appears, and that is what defines decompensated shock. So the "most initial sign" of decompensation is a fall in blood pressure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anuria follows the drop in BP as renal perfusion fails; choose it only if hypotension is not offered.
B. Decreased oxygen delivery to tissues is the underlying mechanism of all shock, present from the start, not a clinical sign of decompensation.
D. Cold and pale skin reflects compensatory vasoconstriction and is already present in compensated shock.
key_concept:
Compensated vs decompensated shock.
  • Compensated: normal BP, tachycardia, cool skin, reduced urine output.
  • Decompensated: hypotension, worsening acidosis, anuria.
  • Irreversible: multiorgan failure, refractory to inotropes.
exam_pearl: Earliest sign of shock is tachycardia; earliest sign of decompensation is hypotension.

stem: female with upper and med pubic tubercle swelling irreducible , type of hernia
why_right: A swelling above and medial to the pubic tubercle is an inguinal hernia, whatever the patient's sex; that location alone excludes a femoral hernia. The swelling is "irreducible", and of the two options the key is obstructed inguinal hernia; strictly, the obstructed label requires bowel obstruction features such as vomiting and distension.
why_wrong_block: A. Strangulated femoral hernia: a femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and strangulation needs a tense, very tender swelling with red skin and systemic signs; neither the site nor these features are described.
key_concept:
Groin hernia by relation to the pubic tubercle.
  • Above and medial: inguinal (direct or indirect).
  • Below and lateral: femoral (more common in women than men, especially elderly multiparous; highest strangulation risk). Inguinal is still the commonest groin hernia in women.
  • Irreducible: cannot be reduced, not tender, no obstruction.
  • Obstructed: irreducible with vomiting, distension, air fluid levels.
  • Strangulated: tense, very tender, discolored, systemic toxicity.
exam_pearl: Female sex tempts "femoral", but the site relative to the pubic tubercle decides.

stem: A patient presented with right iliac fossa pain, and description typical of appendicitis she did CT it shows Appendiceal mass with no collection WBC 15
key_concept:
Complicated appendicitis is managed by what CT shows.

  • Mass/phlegmon, no collection: conservative (IV antibiotics)
  • Abscess (collection): percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics
  • Both mass and abscess routes end in interval appendectomy
  • Generalised peritonitis or deterioration: surgery
exam_pearl: The words "no collection" turn a drainage question into a conservative-management question.

stem: A child born post term, what is the neonatologist expected to find most in the baby?
why_right: A post-term baby has lost the protective vernix and is exposed to placental insufficiency, so the classic finding is dry, peeling, cracked, wrinkled skin (postmaturity or dysmaturity). This is the feature most expected on examination.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lanugo (fine body hair) is abundant in preterm babies and is largely shed by term; a post-term baby has little or none.
B. Placental insufficiency in postmaturity causes loss of subcutaneous fat and a wasted look; macrosomia can occur, but increased body fat is not the characteristic finding.
D. Post-term babies have long fingernails; short nails suggest prematurity.
key_concept:
Preterm vs post-term newborn signs.
  • Preterm: abundant lanugo, thin translucent skin, short nails, few sole creases
  • Post-term: dry peeling skin, little vernix and lanugo, long nails, alert wasted look
  • Post-term risks: meconium staining and aspiration, oligohydramnios, hypoglycaemia
exam_pearl: Lanugo and short nails point to preterm; dry peeling skin and long nails point to post-term.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer Is "Dry, Peeling, Wrinkled Skin" A Complication Of Post-Maturity (Specially To Diabetic Mothers)

stem: A baby boy received a vaccine and, after 3 days, developed a torso rash with mild fever (38.5 °C). He is otherwise well, tolerating oral intake, and physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
key_concept:
Post-vaccine rash: match timing and vaccine type.
  • Minutes to hours, urticaria or angioedema: allergy or anaphylaxis
  • 1 to 2 days after inactivated vaccine: fever, local reaction
  • About 1 to 2 weeks after MMR, up to about 3 to 4 weeks after varicella: fever and rash from the live virus
  • Mild reaction or fever after a dose is not a contraindication to the next dose
  • Anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component is an absolute contraindication
exam_pearl: Anaphylaxis to a prior dose or component is the key absolute contraindication; mild fever and rash after a dose do not stop future doses.

stem: 3 Years Old Post TEF Repair, Present With Brassy Cough, 2 Days Earlier He Had Runny Nose, Normal Vitals, Good Air Entry Bilaterally With Expiratory Wheeze?
why_right: Tracheomalacia is the expected sequela of TEF repair: the trachea at the fistula site has weak cartilage and collapses on expiration, giving the classic brassy cough and expiratory wheeze. A simple viral cold ("runny nose 2 days earlier") makes it more noticeable, while the child stays well with normal vitals and good air entry.
why_wrong_block:
A. Asthma gives recurrent episodic wheeze with atopy and response to bronchodilators; it does not explain a brassy cough tied to a repaired TEF.
C. Croup gives a barking cough with inspiratory stridor, hoarseness and often fever and distress after a coryzal prodrome; here the noise is expiratory and the child is stable.
key_concept:
Post-TEF repair + brassy cough + expiratory wheeze = tracheomalacia.
  • Tracheomalacia: dynamic collapse of intrathoracic trachea, expiratory noise; diagnosis by bronchoscopy
  • Laryngomalacia: inspiratory stridor in early infancy, worse supine and with feeding; laryngoscopy
  • Croup: barky cough, inspiratory stridor, 6 months to 3 years
  • Other post-TEF problems: anastomotic stricture (dysphagia), recurrent fistula (cough with feeds), GERD
exam_pearl: Inspiratory stridor points above the thoracic inlet (larynx, croup); expiratory wheeze with brassy cough after TEF points to intrathoracic tracheomalacia.

stem: A guy came from an RTA; did FAST and it shows fluid around the spleen and liver; blood pressure 96/80.
highlight_terms_source: fluid around the spleen and liver
why_right: After blunt trauma, the FAST pathway splits by haemodynamic status: positive FAST in a stable patient goes to CT to grade the solid organ injury, while positive FAST in an unstable patient goes to laparotomy. This recall treats "BP 96/80" (systolic above 90) as haemodynamically stable, so CT is the keyed next step.
why_wrong_block: B. Laparotomy: right for positive FAST in an UNSTABLE patient (persistent hypotension or non-responder to fluids), or for peritonitis or evisceration; this card frames the patient as stable.
key_concept:
Blunt abdominal trauma: FAST result + stability decides the next step.
  • Stable, FAST positive: CT abdomen
  • Stable, FAST negative: observe/re-examine
  • Unstable, FAST positive: laparotomy
  • Unstable, FAST negative: DPL / look for other bleeding source
  • Unstable stab wound: laparotomy without FAST
exam_pearl: If the stem says hypotensive or not responding to fluids, the same positive FAST flips the answer to laparotomy.

stem: A child following up for being tall, has high arm span and long fingers, following up with ophthalmology for eye issues (written like this), no mental retardation. Most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: high arm span and long fingers
why_right: Tall stature, long arm span and long fingers (arachnodactyly) with eye problems needing ophthalmology follow up (myopia, ectopia lentis) and normal intelligence is Marfan syndrome. Normal cognition is what separates it from homocystinuria, which has a similar marfanoid body.
why_wrong_block:
B. Homocystinuria gives a marfanoid habitus with lens dislocation too, but adds intellectual disability and thrombosis; this child has no mental retardation.
C. Loeys-Dietz causes aortic aneurysms with hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate and arterial tortuosity; lens dislocation is not a feature, so the eye clue does not fit.
D. Ehlers-Danlos gives skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility and easy bruising; it is not defined by tall stature, long arm span or lens problems.
key_concept:
Marfanoid body: sort by eye and IQ.
  • Marfan: autosomal dominant, FBN1; upward lens dislocation, myopia, aortic root dilation, MVP, normal IQ
  • Homocystinuria: autosomal recessive; downward lens dislocation, intellectual disability, thrombosis
  • Loeys-Dietz: hypertelorism, bifid uvula, arterial tortuosity, aggressive aneurysms
  • Ehlers-Danlos: stretchy skin, hypermobile joints, poor wound healing
exam_pearl: Marfanoid child plus intellectual disability or thrombosis flips the answer to homocystinuria.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Tall stature + no eye symptoms = EDS; tall stature + eye symptoms = Marfan; tall stature + eye symptoms + retardation = Homocystinuria.

stem: 24-year-old woman with recurrent on-off PR bleeding after defecation. She has spontaneously reduced hemorrhoids. Hb was low. On examination: 3 hemorrhoids at 2, 7, 10 o'clock. How would you manage?
why_right: The keyed answer rests on the classic indications for haemorrhoidectomy: besides grade III to IV disease, bleeding severe enough to cause anaemia ("Hb was low") and failure of non-operative treatment ("recurrent on-off" bleeding) are surgical indications. She also has all three primary haemorrhoid columns involved ("2, 7, 10 o'clock"), favouring a definitive excisional operation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observation: acceptable only for minor, asymptomatic haemorrhoids; recurrent bleeding with anaemia needs treatment.
B. Band ligation: right for grade I to III internal haemorrhoids bleeding without anaemia, as an outpatient first procedure; here the anaemic, recurrent bleeding is treated as an indication for surgery.
D. Conservative: fibre, stool softeners and sitz baths fit grade I to II haemorrhoids with mild symptoms; it will not reliably control bleeding that has already caused anaemia.
key_concept:
Haemorrhoid treatment ladder by grade and complications.
  • Grade I to II: conservative (fibre, softeners, sitz baths)
  • Grade III (manually reduced): band ligation / sclerotherapy
  • Grade IV or failed outpatient procedures: haemorrhoidectomy
  • Bleeding causing anaemia or mixed haemorrhoids: haemorrhoidectomy
  • Older patient or red flags (weight loss, change in bowel habit): colonoscopy first
exam_pearl: "Low Hb" from haemorrhoidal bleeding escalates even low-grade haemorrhoids to surgery in this exam's key.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Textbook excerpt: indications for haemorrhoidectomy include third- and fourth-degree haemorrhoids, second-degree not cured by non-operative treatment, mixed haemorrhoids with well-defined external component, and bleeding causing anaemia. A second version (next page): manual reduction (grade 3), 3 hemorrhoids at 2,7,10 o'clock, Hb and all labs normal, definitive treatment? 'Answer is Hemorrhoidectomy, Period'.

stem: 7-month-old pt. His mother noticed that he stopped smiling, low activity, fatigue. On examination he had multiple movements of neck flexion followed by extension of body & limbs lasting 1-2 seconds in a repetitive pattern. EEG showed slow wave & multifocal spikes (not sure, but it wasn't hypsarrhythmia or chaotic pattern). What's the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: multiple movements of neck flexion followed by extension of body & limbs lasting 1-2 seconds
why_right: A 7-month-old with developmental regression ("stopped smiling", low activity) and brief repetitive flexion then extension spasms of neck, trunk and limbs lasting 1 to 2 seconds in clusters is infantile spasms (West syndrome). The EEG described, slow waves with multifocal spikes, is in fact what hypsarrhythmia consists of, so even an imperfect recall fits the triad of spasms, regression and abnormal EEG.
why_wrong_block:
A. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy starts in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks of the arms and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, normal development and generalized polyspike-wave EEG; it does not occur at 7 months.
C. Lennox-Gastaut presents later (usually 1 to 8 years) with multiple seizure types (tonic, atonic, atypical absence), intellectual disability and slow spike-wave EEG; West syndrome often evolves into it.
key_concept:
Infant + clustered flexor/extensor spasms + regression = West syndrome.
  • Age: peak 4 to 8 months
  • Triad: infantile spasms, developmental arrest/regression, hypsarrhythmia
  • Hypsarrhythmia: chaotic high-voltage slow waves with multifocal spikes
  • Look for tuberous sclerosis (ash leaf spots, Wood lamp)
  • Treatment: ACTH or high-dose steroids; vigabatrin first line in tuberous sclerosis
  • Lennox-Gastaut: childhood, multiple seizure types, slow spike-wave
exam_pearl: Same spasms in a teenager on waking are myoclonic jerks (JME); age is the first clue in childhood epilepsy syndromes.

stem: Surgeon is performing a back lipoma excision under local anesthesia using lidocaine. He suspects an excessive dose of lidocaine may have been administered. What is the earliest sign of lidocaine toxicity?
why_right: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity follows a dose-related sequence: CNS excitation appears first, then seizures, then CNS and cardiovascular depression. The earliest features are subjective CNS symptoms such as circumoral and tongue numbness, metallic taste, lightheadedness and tinnitus, so tinnitus is the earliest sign among the options.
why_wrong_block:
A. Skin rash: suggests allergy, which is rare with amide anaesthetics like lidocaine (more often due to preservatives or ester agents); it is not part of the toxicity sequence.
B. Bradycardia: a cardiovascular sign that appears late, at higher plasma levels, after the CNS features.
C. Seizures: occur after the early prodromal symptoms as levels rise further; they are a sign of established, not early, toxicity.
key_concept:
Lidocaine toxicity runs from CNS excitation to CNS/CVS collapse.
  • Early: perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, lightheadedness
  • Then: visual disturbance, muscle twitching, confusion
  • Then: seizures
  • Late: coma, respiratory arrest, bradyarrhythmia, cardiovascular collapse
  • Treatment: stop injection, ABC, benzodiazepine for seizures, lipid emulsion
exam_pearl: "Earliest" asks for the subjective prodrome (tinnitus, perioral numbness), not the dramatic seizure.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler: Tinnitus. Related 'Q:' on next page: face laceration repaired with lidocaine, most common side effect? A. Nystagmus B. Tinnitus C. Ventricular tachycardia D. Tonic-clonic seizures; Tinnitus highlighted.

stem: A mother brings her 6-month-old baby with pancytopenia and organomegaly. Labs show low hemoglobin. What is the most likely type of leukemia?
why_right: A child with pancytopenia, organomegaly and low hemoglobin has bone marrow replacement with extramedullary infiltration, typical of acute leukemia. ALL is the most common childhood leukemia (and the most common childhood cancer), so it is the most likely type.
why_wrong_block:
A. AML is the second most common childhood leukemia; favour it when the stem gives myeloid clues such as Auer rods, gum infiltration or DIC.
B. CML is rare in children and presents with marked leukocytosis and splenomegaly in the chronic phase, not pancytopenia.
D. Acute non-lymphoblastic leukemia is another name for AML, which is less common than ALL in children.
key_concept:
Child + pancytopenia + hepatosplenomegaly/lymphadenopathy = think acute leukemia; ALL is the most common.
  • ALL: most common childhood leukemia, peak in early childhood
  • AML (= acute non-lymphoblastic): second most common
  • CML: rare in children
exam_pearl: 'Acute non-lymphoblastic' is just AML in old wording; do not treat it as a separate answer.

Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1925).
Compiler note: Screenshot version: 'Which leukemia is the most common in pediatric age group?' with **C. Acute lymphoblastic marked.

stem: Pt bipolar type 1, currently manic episode, best initial?
OptB: "Drug name" to control the manic episode (forgot the name, maybe clozapine or another thing)

Acute mania: choose by severity, and stop any antidepressant.
  • Mild to moderate: lithium, valproate or an antipsychotic alone
  • Severe or agitated: antipsychotic plus lithium or valproate; short term benzodiazepine for agitation
  • Valproate is avoided in women of childbearing potential
  • Lithium monitoring: serum levels, renal and thyroid function
exam_pearl: "Rapid control" or severe agitation points to an antipsychotic; "mood stabilizer" or long term control points to lithium.

stem: Pt with long history of depressive episodes and positive family history of bipolar disorder, now has pressured speech and insomnia. What is the further management?
OptA: Mood stabilizer like clonazepam to prevent mania
OptD: Health education or something like this

Depression plus family history of bipolar plus manic features means suspect bipolar disorder.

  • Management: mood stabilizer or antipsychotic, stop antidepressant
  • Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar depression can trigger mania

stem: A 3-year-old child is seen in the clinic with fever and cough for 5 days following a flu-like prodrome. On examination, there is decreased air entry and crackles over the right lung middle zone. Chest X-ray is performed along with laboratory investigations. BP 90/64 mmHg, HR 110/min, RR 20/min, Temp 36.6 °C, SpO2 97%. Labs: Hb 12 g/dL, platelets 328 x10^9/L, WBC 22 x10^9/L, neutrophils 84%, lymphocytes 15%. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: crackles over the right lung middle zone
why_right: Fever and cough for 5 days with focal crackles and reduced air entry over the right middle zone, WBC 22 with 84% neutrophils, is bacterial community-acquired pneumonia, which needs antibiotics. The child is stable: SpO2 97%, normal RR and BP, no distress, so it is mild pneumonia managed at home with oral amoxicillin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance fits a viral URTI; focal chest signs with neutrophilic leukocytosis mean bacterial pneumonia that needs antibiotics.
B. Bronchodilator and steroids treat asthma or wheeze; this child has focal crackles, not diffuse wheeze.
C. Admission for IV antibiotics is for severe pneumonia: SpO2 below 92%, respiratory distress, tachypnea, inability to take oral fluids, toxic look or complications such as empyema; none are present.
key_concept:
Pediatric CAP: severity decides where and how.
  • Mild (well, SpO2 ≥92%, feeding): oral amoxicillin at home
  • Severe: hypoxia, grunting, retractions, poor feeding, toxicity: admit, IV antibiotics, oxygen
  • First-line oral drug: amoxicillin (covers pneumococcus)
  • Stony dullness suggests parapneumonic effusion
exam_pearl: Hypoxia (SpO2 below 92%) is the single sign that flips management from oral home treatment to admission.

stem: Patient post op with fever and reduced lung expansion. Diagnosis?
why_right: Post-operative fever with "reduced lung expansion" is the picture of atelectasis: pain and diaphragmatic splinting cause shallow breathing and alveolar collapse. It is the classic cause of fever in the first post-operative day, and the stem gives no productive cough or consolidation to suggest infection.
why_wrong_block: B. Pneumonia: typically days 2 to 3 onward, often from untreated atelectasis, with productive cough, crackles or bronchial breathing and consolidation on X-ray; none of these are described.
key_concept:
Post-operative fever by timing ("5 Ws").
  • Day 1: atelectasis (wind)
  • Days 2 to 3: pneumonia, UTI (water), thrombophlebitis
  • Days 5 to 7: wound infection, anastomotic leak/abscess
  • Day 7+: DVT/PE (walking), drug fever
  • Atelectasis: incentive spirometry, analgesia, early mobilisation
exam_pearl: Fever with reduced expansion in the first day is atelectasis; productive cough with consolidation from day 3 onward points to pneumonia.

stem: Triceps mass? Suggestive of malignant. Investigation?
key_concept:
Suspected limb sarcoma: image, then biopsy, then stage.
  • Local imaging: MRI of the mass
  • Biopsy of choice: core needle (usually image guided)
  • Small superficial lesion: excisional biopsy
  • Large lesion, core not available: incisional biopsy along the resection line
  • Staging: CT chest
exam_pearl: If core needle biopsy appears as an option, it beats both excisional and incisional biopsy for a suspected limb sarcoma.

stem: Patient after RTA with severe lower back pain (suspected spinal fracture), what to do until the surgeon comes?
highlight_terms_source: what to do until the surgeon comes
why_right: In a trauma patient with a suspected spinal fracture, the immediate priority while awaiting the surgeon is restriction of spinal movement (log roll, collar, supine on a firm surface) to prevent secondary cord injury. This is part of the primary survey and stays in place until the spine is cleared, usually by CT.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT whole spine: the imaging used to clear or define the injury, but it comes after immobilisation and the primary survey; it does not replace protecting the spine "until the surgeon comes".
B. Flexion extension test: dangerous in an acute suspected fracture because it can displace an unstable segment; reserved for later assessment of ligamentous instability in an alert patient with normal initial imaging.
D. Pelvic binder: right for a suspected unstable pelvic fracture with haemodynamic instability; the stem describes lower back pain without pelvic instability or shock.
key_concept:
Suspected spinal injury: protect first, image second.
  • Primary survey with spinal motion restriction
  • Log roll, rigid collar for cervical spine, firm flat surface
  • CT is the imaging of choice to clear the spine
  • MRI for cord or ligamentous injury
  • Never perform dynamic (flexion/extension) views acutely
exam_pearl: "What to do until the surgeon comes" asks for immobilisation, not an investigation.

stem: Amoebic liver abscess initial management.
why_right: Amoebic liver abscess responds well to metronidazole, which is the initial management even when the abscess is large. Drainage is not needed in most patients because the tissue amoebicide clears the infection, followed by a luminal agent to eradicate gut cysts.
why_wrong_block: A. Percutaneous drainage: right for a PYOGENIC liver abscess, or for an amoebic abscess that fails to respond to metronidazole, is at risk of rupture (for example left lobe near the pericardium), or when the diagnosis is uncertain.
key_concept:
Liver abscess: the organism decides the first step.
  • Amoebic (E. histolytica): metronidazole, then luminal agent
  • Pyogenic: IV antibiotics + percutaneous drainage
  • Hydatid: albendazole, then PAIR or surgery
  • Amoebic clues: travel to endemic area, dysentery, solitary lesion
exam_pearl: "Amoebic" in the stem means drug first even for a large abscess; "pyogenic" means drain.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' version on next page: most appropriate initial treatment for a liver amoebic abscess? A. Metronidazole B. Open drainage C. Percutaneous drainage D. Percutaneous aspiration. Answer: A.

stem: DM with wound, delayed closure, 10 cm open wound with granulation tissue seen. Management?
OptB: Antibiotics cream or something like this
why_right: A large ("10 cm") open diabetic wound with healthy "granulation tissue" and "delayed closure" is clean but slow to heal, which is the ideal setting for vacuum-assisted (negative pressure) closure. It removes exudate, reduces oedema and promotes granulation and wound contraction, preparing the bed for closure or grafting.
why_wrong_block:
A. Dressing: standard moist dressings suit small or uncomplicated wounds; this large wound has already shown delayed healing, so it needs an active healing adjunct.
B. Antibiotic cream: indicated only for local infection; a clean granulating wound has no infection to treat, and topical antibiotics do not speed closure.
key_concept:
Match wound treatment to the wound bed.
  • Necrotic or slough: debridement first
  • Infected: debridement + systemic antibiotics
  • Clean granulating, large or slow healing: negative pressure wound therapy
  • Healthy granulating bed ready: skin graft or delayed closure
  • Diabetic foot: offloading and glycaemic control throughout
exam_pearl: If the wound has necrotic tissue, the answer becomes debridement (then VAC), not VAC alone.

stem: A patient post hernia (mesh) repair: what is the advice to prevent recurrence of hernia?
OptC: Avoid lifting heavy objects for 6 months
why_right: After a mesh hernia repair, recurrence is driven by raised intra-abdominal pressure loading the repair before the mesh is fully incorporated into scar tissue. The lead-in asks for advice to prevent recurrence, and avoiding heavy lifting and straining is the classic counselling point; this recall keys a 6-month restriction.
why_wrong_block:
A. A compression bandage or binder may be offered for comfort or seroma control in the first weeks, but it does not protect the repair, and 3 months of compression is not standard advice.
B. Avoiding constipation and straining is sensible in the early post-operative period (especially with opioids), but routine laxatives for 6 months are not recommended; treat constipation if it occurs.
key_concept:
Post-hernia repair counselling targets factors that raise intra-abdominal pressure.
  • Avoid heavy lifting and straining while the repair heals
  • Treat constipation, chronic cough and urinary straining (e.g. BPH)
  • Stop smoking and lose weight: both raise recurrence
  • Return to light daily activity early is encouraged
exam_pearl: The exam answer for preventing recurrence is the activity restriction (no heavy lifting), not a device or a drug.

stem: Patient you want to repair their carpal tunnel hand; after you inject lidocaine and epinephrine the patient starts to have pain and pale hand. What will help you to establish the diagnosis?
OptC: Monitor blood pressure and heart rates
why_right: Pain and a pale hand right after injecting lidocaine with epinephrine point to epinephrine-induced vasoconstriction causing local ischemia. The lead-in asks what will help you establish the diagnosis, so the step is a bedside assessment of the hand for ischemia: colour, temperature, capillary refill and pulses.
why_wrong_block:
B. Phentolamine (local infiltration) is the treatment that reverses epinephrine vasoconstriction once ischemia is confirmed; it does not establish the diagnosis.
C. Monitoring BP and heart rate looks for systemic epinephrine or local anaesthetic toxicity (tachycardia, hypertension); it would be right if the symptoms were systemic, but the finding here is local hand pallor.
D. Doppler ultrasound is not needed first; clinical examination of perfusion establishes ischemia at the bedside, and imaging is reserved for unclear or persistent cases.
key_concept:
Epinephrine in hand blocks: diagnose clinically, treat with phentolamine.
  • Pale, cold, painful digits after epinephrine = vasoconstrictive ischemia
  • Diagnosis: inspect colour, capillary refill, temperature, pulses
  • Treatment: local phentolamine infiltration (alpha blocker), warming
  • Systemic features (palpitations, hypertension) = monitor vitals
exam_pearl: "Establish the diagnosis" = assess the hand; "treat/reverse" = phentolamine.

stem: A child was rescued from a house fire and was noted to have soot around the mouth and nose. What is the most likely type of injury?
highlight_terms_source: soot around the mouth and nose
why_right: A child rescued from a house fire with soot around the mouth and nose has a marker of inhalation of smoke and hot gases, i.e. inhalation injury. Soot or carbonaceous material in the airway (and carbonaceous sputum) is the most telling sign of inhalation injury and is itself an indication to secure the airway early.
why_wrong_block: A. Carbon monoxide poisoning often coexists in enclosed-space fires, but it is a systemic toxicity diagnosed by carboxyhaemoglobin level (headache, confusion, drowsiness); soot on the face indicates airway exposure, not CO toxicity itself.
key_concept:
Fire victim: look for airway injury first.
  • Signs: soot/carbonaceous sputum, singed facial or nasal hair, facial burn, hoarseness, stridor, wheeze
  • Highest diagnostic value: carbonaceous sputum/soot in airway
  • Intubate early if: facial burn, airway oedema, soot in airway, respiratory failure, extensive burns, altered consciousness
  • Also check COHb and give 100% oxygen
exam_pearl: Soot or singed hair = inhalation injury; drowsiness with a high COHb = CO poisoning (they often coexist).
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' version: boy pulled out from a house fire, distressed with carbonaceous sputum, wheeze, hoarseness, facial burn; A. Esophageal tear B. Inhalation injury C. CO2 poisoning D. Fracture of face bones; B highlighted.

stem: An elderly man presents with bright red blood per rectum mixed with stool. His hemoglobin is low. What is the next best step?
highlight_terms_source: bright red blood per rectum mixed with stool
why_right: An elderly man with bright red blood per rectum and a low hemoglobin has a significant lower GI bleed, and the full version of this recall adds hypotension (BP 90/40). In any acute GI bleed with instability, the first step is resuscitation: large-bore IV access, fluids and blood transfusion, before any diagnostic procedure. Hypotension from bleeding is an indication to transfuse regardless of the exact Hb value.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colonoscopy is the main diagnostic and therapeutic tool for lower GI bleeding, but only once the patient is stabilized and bowel prep is possible.
B. CT angiography localizes active bleeding and is the next test in an unstable lower GI bleed after stabilization, not before resuscitation.
C. NG aspiration/EGD is used when an upper source is suspected (melena, haematemesis, or brisk hematochezia with shock); it still follows resuscitation.
key_concept:
GI bleeding: ABC and resuscitation before localization.
  • Unstable: stabilize (2 large-bore IVs, fluids, blood products, reverse anticoagulants), then CT angiography
  • Stable: colonoscopy after bowel prep
  • Source not found: CT angiography or colonoscopy, then tagged RBC scan / small bowel evaluation
  • Brisk hematochezia with shock: exclude an upper source
exam_pearl: If the options mix a test with resuscitation and the patient is unstable or anaemic, resuscitation comes first.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot version adds BP 90/40, with answer D. Supportive care IV fluids, transfusion, resuscitation. Compiler: Hb was not mentioned in numbers, just said 'low'; hypotension is indication for transfusion regardless of values (even if above 7).

stem: 45-year-old man is complaining of chills and rigors. He underwent an elective subtotal colectomy for ulcerative colitis 12 hours ago (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 110/min, Respiratory rate 18/min, Temperature 38°C. Test Result: Hb (110-170 g/L Male, 120-160 g/L Female), HCT (0.40-0.52 Male, 0.37-0.48 Female), WBC 15 (4.5-10.5 x 109/L), Neutrophils 60 (40-60%). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The patient meets 2 SIRS criteria: heart rate 110 (above 90) and WBC 15 (above 12). Temperature 38 is not above 38 and RR 18 is not above 20. Only 12 hours after an elective colectomy, no infection source is identified, so this is SIRS from the surgical insult rather than sepsis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sepsis requires SIRS plus a confirmed or suspected infection (e.g. positive urine culture, infected stent); none is stated here.
B. Bacteremia is the answer when a postoperative infection is suspected but no SIRS criteria are met; this patient meets two.
C. Severe sepsis requires sepsis plus organ dysfunction (e.g. collapse needing ICU, hypotension); BP is 110/70 with no organ failure.
key_concept:
SIRS = 2 or more criteria; then add infection and organ failure.
  • Temp <36 or >38 C; HR >90; RR >20 or PaCO2 <32; WBC <4 or >12 or >10% bands
  • SIRS + infection = sepsis
  • Sepsis + organ dysfunction = severe sepsis
  • Severe sepsis + refractory hypotension = septic shock
  • Suspected infection, no SIRS criteria = bacteremia
exam_pearl: Early post-op (first 24 h) with no source = SIRS; the same numbers plus a positive culture = sepsis.

stem: A 25 year old male with bilateral breast enlargement since the age of 18, he's uncomfortable and reluctant to swim or exercise at the gym PE revealed grade 4 gynecomastia, most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: uncomfortable and reluctant to swim or exercise
why_right: A 25-year-old with gynecomastia present since age 18 has persistent pubertal gynecomastia that will not regress, and grade 4 (severe) enlargement causing distress and avoidance of swimming and the gym. Long-standing (fibrotic) gynecomastia does not respond to medical therapy, so the definitive treatment is surgical: subcutaneous mastectomy, often combined with liposuction.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance fits pubertal gynecomastia in adolescents, which usually regresses within 1 to 2 years; this has persisted for 7 years and is severe and symptomatic.
B. Core biopsy is for a suspicious unilateral, hard, eccentric or fixed mass (male breast cancer); bilateral diffuse enlargement does not need biopsy.
D. Endocrine and liver work-up is right for new-onset adult gynecomastia, rapid growth, or features of an underlying cause (drugs, testicular tumour, liver disease, hypogonadism); this is long-standing since puberty and the question asks for management.
key_concept:
Gynecomastia: duration and severity choose the step.
  • Adolescent, recent: reassure and observe
  • New-onset adult or suspicious features: history (drugs), testicular exam, endocrine and liver tests
  • Early, tender (<12 months): consider medical therapy (e.g. tamoxifen)
  • Long-standing, fibrotic, severe or distressing: subcutaneous mastectomy ± liposuction
  • Unilateral hard mass: imaging and biopsy
exam_pearl: Recent onset in an adult = work-up first; years-long, severe, bothersome = surgery.

stem: 35 YO female patient presented to the screening clinic, her mother diagnosed with Breast cancer at age of 43 and her father with colon cancer at age of 53, what you will do for her?
OptD: Mammogram at age of 40 and colonoscopy at age of 55
highlight_terms_source: mother diagnosed with Breast cancer at age of 43
father with colon cancer at age of 53
why_right: A 35-year-old whose mother had breast cancer at 43 is at increased (family history) risk, so screening starts early rather than at the average-risk age: about 10 years before the relative's age at diagnosis (here 33), but not before 30. She is already past that age, so she should start annual mammography now.
why_wrong_block:
B. Starting at 40 is the average-risk schedule; a first-degree relative diagnosed at 43 moves her start earlier.
C. This option was not recalled, so it cannot be assessed.
D. Both parts are wrong: mammography should start now, and a father with colon cancer before 60 means colonoscopy from age 40 (or 10 years before his diagnosis), repeated every 5 years, not at 55.
key_concept:
Family history pulls screening earlier.
  • Breast, first-degree relative: annual mammogram from 10 years before her diagnosis age, not before 30
  • Average-risk breast (Saudi MOH): mammogram from 40, every 1 to 2 years
  • Colorectal, first-degree relative <60: colonoscopy at 40 or 10 years earlier, every 5 years
  • Average-risk colorectal: start at 45
exam_pearl: Subtract 10 from the relative's diagnosis age: if the patient is already older, screen now.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler notes on mammogram intervals: ACS guidelines >45 every year, >55 every 2 years; Saudi guidelines >40 every 1 or 2 years, >50 every 2 years.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has just completed her screening mammogram and the results were normal. She has no symptoms and no family history of breast cancer. When she should have another mammogram?
highlight_terms_source: no symptoms and no family history
why_right: She is 55, asymptomatic, with no family history and a normal screening mammogram, so she is average risk. For average-risk women in this age group the interval is every 2 years (Saudi screening from 50 is biennial; ACS moves to every 2 years from 55).
why_wrong_block:
A. A 6-month follow-up mammogram is for a BI-RADS 3 (probably benign) finding, not a normal result.
B. Annual screening applies to higher-risk women or to the younger screening band (e.g. ACS 45 to 54); at 55 with average risk it is biennial.
D. A 3-year interval is the cervical cytology schedule, not breast screening.
key_concept:
Average-risk mammography intervals.
  • Saudi: 40 to 50 every 1 to 2 years; above 50 every 2 years
  • ACS: 45 to 54 yearly; 55 and above every 2 years (or yearly by choice)
  • BI-RADS 3: short-interval follow-up at 6 months
  • Higher risk (family history, genes): annual, starting earlier
exam_pearl: Normal result + 55 + average risk = 2 years; 6 months is only for BI-RADS 3.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot within block 1710. ACS Guidelines: >45 every year, >55 every 2 years. Saudi Guidelines: >40 every 1 or 2 years, >50 every 2 years.

stem: A 50-year-old man underwent an open mesh repair of a left inguinal hernia. He presented 2 months later because he noticed that the left testes had become smaller in size. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
why_right: Testicular atrophy appearing 2 months after an open inguinal hernia repair is classically from ischemic orchitis, caused by thrombosis of the pampiniform venous plexus from dissection of the spermatic cord. Venous congestion first gives a swollen, tender testis in the early days, then atrophy over the following months.
why_wrong_block:
A. Testicular artery injury is uncommon and rarely causes atrophy because collateral flow from the cremasteric and vasal (deferential) arteries keeps the testis viable.
B. Mesh migration is rare and presents with pain, mass, fistula or bowel/bladder erosion, not testicular atrophy.
D. An overly tight external (superficial) ring could compress the cord, but this is not the recognized mechanism; the venous thrombosis from cord dissection is.
key_concept:
Ischemic orchitis after hernia repair is venous.
  • Cause: thrombosis of pampiniform plexus from cord dissection
  • Early (days): painful swollen testis
  • Late (weeks to months): testicular atrophy
  • Higher risk with extensive cord dissection and recurrent hernia repair
exam_pearl: Atrophy after hernia repair = veins (pampiniform thrombosis), not the artery, because of arterial collaterals.

stem: Female pt (can't remember her age) her BMI 35, going to do surgery asking about VTE prophylaxis?
key_concept:
VTE prophylaxis: match intensity to risk, check bleeding and kidneys.
  • Low risk: early mobilization ± mechanical
  • Moderate/high risk (obesity, major surgery, cancer, immobility): LMWH, e.g. enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily
  • High bleeding risk: mechanical until safe to start drug
  • Renal impairment: unfractionated heparin instead of LMWH
  • Severe obesity: dose adjustment may be considered
exam_pearl: Deciding fork: major surgery with no bleeding risk favours LMWH (± stockings); minor surgery or high bleeding risk favours mechanical prophylaxis alone.

stem: A 40-year-old diabetic patient complains of a painful perianal swelling with fever for the last 3 days (see lab results). Blood pressure: 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate: 110/min, Respiratory rate: 20/min, Temperature: 38 °C. Test Result Normal Values: Hb: 135 (130-170 g/L for Male, 120-160 g/L for Female), WBC: 16 (4.5-10.5 x 10^9/L), Neutrophils: 80 (40-60%), Random Glucose: 6.5 (3.9-5.5 mmol/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A painful perianal swelling for 3 days with fever 38 °C, tachycardia 110/min and leukocytosis (WBC 16, neutrophils 80%) is a perianal abscess. The systemic inflammatory response is the decisive clue that separates an infected collection from a simple painful lump. Diabetes is a classic risk factor for perianal sepsis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anal fissure causes sharp pain during and after defecation with fresh bleeding; there is no swelling, fever or raised WBC.
B. Internal hemorrhoids present with painless fresh bleeding after defecation, not a tender swelling with fever and leukocytosis.
D. Thrombosed piles give an acutely painful bluish swelling but the patient is afebrile with a normal WBC; fever plus neutrophilia points to pus.
key_concept:
Painful perianal lump: look at temperature and WBC first.
  • Lump + fever + leukocytosis = perianal abscess (incision and drainage)
  • Lump + normal vitals and WBC = perianal hematoma / thrombosed external pile
  • Pain on defecation + fresh blood, no lump = anal fissure
  • Painless fresh bleeding = internal hemorrhoids
  • Persistent discharge after a lump ruptured = fistula in ano
exam_pearl: Same painful lump but afebrile with normal WBC flips the answer to perianal hematoma.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall: "perianal abscess diagnosis clear". Compiler attached two screenshots on the next page (this one and a 30-year-old afebrile variant).

stem: A 30-year-old presented with a 3-day history of painful perianal swelling. Examination confirmed a 1x1 cm tender swelling close to the anal verge (see lab result). Heart rate 84/min, Temperature 37.2 °C. Test Result Normal Value: WBC 8 (4.5-10.5 x 10^9/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: 1x1 cm tender swelling close to the anal verge
why_right: A small (1x1 cm) tender swelling at the anal verge for 3 days in a patient with normal heart rate, temperature 37.2 °C and WBC 8 is a perianal hematoma (thrombosed external hemorrhoid). It is painful but there is no systemic inflammatory response, which rules out an abscess.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anal fissure is a linear tear giving sharp pain on defecation and bleeding; it does not produce a palpable swelling.
B. A prolapsed pile is a congested mucosal mass protruding from the anus, not a small tender subcutaneous lump at the verge.
C. Perianal abscess would come with fever, tachycardia and leukocytosis; here vitals and WBC are normal.
key_concept:
Painful perianal lump: vitals and WBC decide.
  • Normal temperature and WBC = perianal hematoma
  • Fever + leukocytosis = perianal abscess
  • Hematoma seen early (within about 72 h) can be evacuated; later it is managed conservatively
exam_pearl: Add fever and a raised WBC to the same lump and the answer becomes perianal abscess.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot under block 1731 (on next page); afebrile with normal WBC points away from abscess.

stem: Fournier's Gangrene DM crepitus and anal cellulitis initial investigation
why_wrong_block:
A. Ultrasound can show subcutaneous gas or scrotal involvement, but it is operator dependent and does not change the need for immediate debridement once crepitus is felt.
B. MRI defines soft tissue extent well but is slow and often unavailable in the emergency setting; waiting for it delays life-saving surgery.
C. CT is the most useful imaging to map gas and the extent of spread in a stable patient when the diagnosis is unclear, but with clinical crepitus it should not postpone debridement.
key_concept:
Fournier gangrene = necrotizing fasciitis of the genitalia and perineum.
  • Risk: diabetes, immunosuppression, perianal or urogenital infection
  • Clues: pain out of proportion, crepitus, dusky skin, bullae, systemic toxicity
  • Polymicrobial (gram positive, gram negative, anaerobes)
  • Treatment: urgent surgical debridement + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics + resuscitation
  • Repeat debridement and later reconstruction as needed
exam_pearl: Crepitus in a diabetic perineum means theatre now; imaging is only for doubtful, stable cases.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer line gives Debridement (not among the listed options).

stem: Elderly, epigastric pain for 3m, wt loss, jaundice and dark urine There was dilatation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct Labs: cholestatic picture (They did not mention if the gallbladder is palpable or shrunk)
highlight_terms_source: wt loss, jaundice and dark urine
dilatation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct
why_right: An elderly patient with 3 months of epigastric pain, weight loss and obstructive jaundice (dark urine, cholestatic labs) suggests malignancy. Dilatation of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts places the obstruction distally at the ampulla, so ampullary cancer fits best. The gallbladder status is not given, so the level of duct dilatation is the decisive clue.
why_wrong_block:
A. Klatskin tumor sits at the hepatic duct confluence, so only intrahepatic ducts dilate and the gallbladder is collapsed; extrahepatic dilatation excludes it.
B. Gallbladder cancer usually shows a gallbladder mass or wall thickening, often with gallstones, and causes jaundice by hilar invasion rather than a distal block with full-length duct dilatation.
key_concept:
Level of biliary dilatation localises the tumour.
  • Intrahepatic only + collapsed GB = Klatskin (hilar cholangiocarcinoma)
  • Intra + extrahepatic + distended GB = distal block (pancreatic head, ampullary, periampullary)
  • Palpable non-tender GB with jaundice = Courvoisier sign, favours malignancy over stones
exam_pearl: If only intrahepatic ducts are dilated, switch to Klatskin tumor.

stem: A 67-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of yellowish discoloration of his sclera and skin with dark urine and pale stool. On examination, he was jaundiced with a palpable distended gallbladder (see report and lab results). Test Result Normal Values: Alkaline phosphatase 421 (39-117 IU/L), Direct bilirubin 122.3 (1.5-6.5 umol/L), Total bilirubin 134.5 (3.5-16.5 umol/L). Ultrasound: Dilated intra and extrahepatic bile ducts with hugely distended gallbladder. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Dilated intra and extrahepatic bile ducts with hugely distended gallbladder
why_right: A 67-year-old man with 2 months of jaundice, dark urine and pale stool has obstructive jaundice (ALP and direct bilirubin high). A palpable distended gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) plus dilated intra and extrahepatic ducts with a hugely distended gallbladder place a malignant block in the distal CBD, classically pancreatic head cancer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Klatskin tumor is at the hepatic duct confluence, giving a shrunken gallbladder and only intrahepatic dilatation.
C. Mirizzi syndrome is a stone impacted in the cystic duct or Hartmann pouch compressing the common hepatic duct, with RUQ pain and cholecystitis features, not painless progressive jaundice with a huge gallbladder.
D. CBD stones give painful, fluctuating jaundice and the gallbladder is usually fibrosed and not palpable (Courvoisier law).
key_concept:
Courvoisier law: jaundice + palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be stones.
  • Distended GB + intra and extrahepatic dilatation = pancreatic head or periampullary tumour
  • Collapsed GB + intrahepatic dilatation only = Klatskin
  • Stones: pain, fluctuating jaundice, fibrosed GB
exam_pearl: Collapsed gallbladder with intrahepatic dilatation only flips the answer to Klatskin tumor.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's "Q:" related version under 1745; Answer: B (MG).

stem: 42-year-old patient undergoes colonoscopy for evaluation of gastrointestinal symptoms. A 1.3 cm colonic polyp is identified and removed. Histopathology reveals a tubular adenoma. What is the most appropriate follow-up colonoscopy interval?
why_right: A single tubular adenoma of 1.3 cm is an advanced adenoma because it is ≥10 mm. Current post-polypectomy surveillance guidance recommends repeat colonoscopy at 3 years for an adenoma ≥10 mm after complete removal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ten years is the interval after a normal colonoscopy, or roughly 7 to 10 years for 1 to 2 small (<10 mm) tubular adenomas; a 1.3 cm adenoma is higher risk.
B. Very short intervals (months) are for incomplete or piecemeal removal of a large polyp, or a malignant polyp, not a completely excised tubular adenoma.
C. An adenoma is a premalignant neoplastic polyp, so surveillance colonoscopy is always needed after removal; even small hyperplastic polyps (<10 mm) still return to routine 10-year screening rather than no follow-up.
key_concept:
Surveillance depends on adenoma size, number and histology.
  • Normal colonoscopy: 10 years
  • 1 to 2 tubular adenomas <10 mm: 7 to 10 years
  • Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous histology or high-grade dysplasia: 3 years
  • Piecemeal removal of a large polyp: early check in about 6 months
  • Malignant risk: villous > tubulovillous > tubular > hyperplastic
exam_pearl: Size ≥10 mm or villous/high-grade dysplasia makes it advanced: 3 years.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1828).

stem: 40~yr, Breast mass for 3 months upper outer quadrant Biopsy option
why_right: A 40-year-old with a 3-month upper outer quadrant breast mass is evaluated by triple assessment; the biopsy of choice for a solid breast mass is core needle (Tru-cut) biopsy. It gives histology with tissue architecture, distinguishes invasive from in situ disease and allows receptor testing before definitive surgery.
why_wrong_block:
A. FNAC gives cytology only and cannot show invasion or receptor status; it is used for cystic lesions or axillary nodes.
C. Excisional biopsy is not first-line for a suspicious mass because it can compromise later definitive surgery; it is used when core biopsy is non-diagnostic or discordant, or for some benign lesions.
key_concept:
Triple assessment: clinical exam + imaging + biopsy.
  • Age >30: mammogram ± ultrasound first
  • Age <30: ultrasound first
  • Solid mass: core needle (Tru-cut) biopsy
  • Cystic mass: fine needle aspiration
exam_pearl: If the question asks the first step (not the biopsy), a woman over 30 gets imaging (mammogram) before biopsy.
